archives-compression: Newcomers reasonably ask why Linux needs two tools where Windows has one, and the answer is a perfect illustration of the philosophy from the very first lesson. Tar does one job: it takes many files and directories and concatenates them into a single stream, preserving permissions, timestamps and ownership. It does not compress at all — a bare tar file is the same size as its contents. Gzip does the other job: it takes one stream and compresses it. It knows nothing about multiple files. Chain them and you get a compressed archive, which is why the extension is dot tar dot gz — it is literally a tar that has then been gzipped. The benefit of separating them is that you can swap the compressor without changing anything else, and that is exactly what happened as better algorithms arrived. Bzip2 gave smaller files more slowly, xz gave smaller still and slower again, and now zstd gives you nearly gzip's speed with close to xz's ratio, which makes it the best default if the machine has it. Zip, by contrast, bundles and compresses in a single format, which is more convenient and less flexible — and it does not preserve Unix permissions properly, which is why you should not use it for anything you intend to restore onto a Linux system.

Tar's flags are famously unmemorable, so use the mnemonic: create ze file, extract ze file, list ze file. C for create, x for extract, t for list, with z for gzip and f meaning the next argument is the filename. That covers essentially everything you will do. The habit worth building is running dash t first on any archive you did not create yourself. Well-behaved archives contain a single top-level directory, so extracting is tidy. Badly made ones — and they are common — have all their files at the top level, and extracting one dumps a hundred loose files directly into your current directory, mixed in with whatever was already there. Cleaning that up is genuinely tedious. Ten seconds of listing tells you which kind you have. Dash capital C extracts into a directory you specify, which saves you from changing directory first and forgetting to change back. The last line is a nice demonstration of the streaming idea: tar writes the archive to standard output instead of a file, and it goes straight over SSH to the remote machine, so a large directory is backed up remotely without ever creating a temporary archive on the local disk — useful when the local disk is the thing that is nearly full.

A few practical things. Gzip on its own replaces the file with a compressed version and removes the original, which surprises people — pass dash k if you want to keep it. But the genuinely valuable items on this slide are the z-prefixed tools. Zcat, zgrep and zless read gzipped files directly, decompressing on the fly in memory. This matters constantly on servers, because log rotation compresses old logs, and the instinct is to gunzip a file so you can search it. Do not. Zgrep searches it in place. On a rotated log directory you can zgrep across every compressed archive at once and never write a single temporary file, which also matters when the disk is short on space — which, given you are probably investigating a full disk, it often is. The last thing to internalize is what compresses and what does not. Text compresses beautifully, often ten to one, so logs, source code, JSON and CSV all shrink dramatically. Data that is already compressed — JPEG images, MP4 video, gzip files, and yes, the mp3 and opus audio on this very site — will not shrink at all, because the redundancy has already been removed. Re-compressing them wastes CPU and occasionally produces a slightly larger file. Knowing which is which saves you from pointless work.

Let us close with the everyday uses. Dating your archive names costs nothing at the time and is enormously helpful six months later when you are looking for the right one to restore, so make it a habit. Listing before extracting we have covered, and it is worth repeating because it takes seconds and prevents a mess. The third one is less well known and quite useful: you can extract a single file out of a large archive by naming its path, without unpacking the whole thing. When you need one configuration file out of a ten gigabyte backup, that saves a great deal of time and disk. And on log rotation — you can absolutely gzip yesterday's log with a cron job, and for a small personal service that is fine. But for anything real, use logrotate, which is already installed on your system. It handles the timing, keeps a configurable number of old logs and deletes the rest, compresses them, preserves the correct ownership and permissions, and crucially it can signal the service afterwards so the program reopens its log file. That last part matters: if you rename a log file underneath a running process, the process keeps writing to the old file by its inode, and your new log stays empty — which is exactly the inode behaviour we met back in Part One.

This is a short lesson because it deserves to be, so let us keep the summary honest. Three tar commands cover almost everything: create, extract, and list. Everything else — the exotic flags, the incremental archive features, the exclusion patterns — you can look up on the rare occasions you need them, and nobody will think less of you for checking the manual. Remember to use the z-prefixed tools on compressed logs rather than decompressing first, because it is faster, uses no disk, and becomes essential precisely when disk is the problem. And remember what is worth compressing: text yes, already-compressed media no. That is the lesson. Next we look at scheduling work with cron and systemd timers, which is how these backup and rotation commands stop being things you remember to run and start being things that simply happen. And after that, the lesson this entire course has been building toward: what a container actually is, which is where every piece of Linux you have learned — processes, filesystems, permissions, namespaces — comes together into a single idea.
bash-loops-functions: Conditionals in bash look strange until you learn one fact: the opening square bracket is not syntax, it is a command. There is literally a program called left-bracket. That explains the thing everyone gets wrong at first, which is that you must put spaces around the brackets — because without them the shell cannot tell where the command name ends. It also explains why the operators look like flags, because they are flags being passed to that command. The test operators split into three families. Numeric comparisons use the dash e q style names. String comparisons use equals and not-equals, plus dash z for empty and dash n for non-empty. And file tests ask questions about the filesystem: dash f for a regular file, dash d for a directory, dash r for readable. Now the recommendation: in bash, use double square brackets instead. They are a shell builtin rather than a command, which means unquoted variables do not word-split inside them, so a whole class of bugs simply disappears. They also let you use the ampersand-ampersand operator directly, match against glob patterns, and do regex matching with the equals-tilde operator. The only reason to use single brackets is if your script must run under plain POSIX sh. And one warning: using equals for numbers compares them as text, so ten is less than nine. It produces a wrong answer, not an error.

For loops over a glob are the bread and butter: for f in star dot log iterates over each matching file, and because the shell expands the glob before the loop starts, this handles filenames correctly as long as you quote the variable inside. Brace expansion gives you numeric ranges, and there is a C-style form when you need an index. Now the important part of this slide, because it is one of the most common bugs in shell scripting. To read a file line by line, do not write for line in dollar open-paren cat file. That looks natural and it is wrong, because the for loop splits on whitespace, not on newlines — so a line containing spaces becomes several iterations, and your loop body runs on fragments. The correct incantation is the while read form, and each piece of it matters. Setting IFS to empty stops leading and trailing whitespace being stripped. Dash r stops backslashes in the data being interpreted as escapes. And the redirect at the end feeds the file in. Memorize that line as a unit; it is worth it. The last example handles filenames from find safely, using null separators so that even names containing newlines survive. And a subtle trap: a glob matching nothing expands to the literal pattern, so your loop runs once with a nonsense filename unless you guard for it.

Functions in bash work the way you would hope, with one significant difference to internalize. Define one with a name, parentheses and braces, and inside it the arguments are the same positional variables a script uses — dollar one, dollar two, quoted dollar at. The difference is what a function returns. The return statement does not return a value; it sets an exit code, an integer from zero to two hundred fifty five, which means success or failure and nothing else. To return actual data, you echo it and the caller captures it with dollar-parenthesis command substitution. Once you accept that, functions become very natural for shell work: because they return exit codes, they compose directly into if-statements, which is exactly what the is-running example does. The three functions at the top of this slide are worth copying into every script you write. Log prints a timestamped message to standard error, so your diagnostics never pollute your output. Die logs and exits, which turns error handling into one short word. And require checks that a dependency exists before you need it, so your script fails immediately with a clear message rather than halfway through with a confusing one. One habit: declare variables inside functions with local, or they are global and will quietly collide.

Two more constructs and you have everything you need. Arrays hold lists, which matters because otherwise people store lists in strings separated by spaces and then get destroyed by a filename containing a space. Declare one with parentheses, index it with square brackets, append with plus-equals. The critical form is the one at the top: quoted, with the at sign inside the brackets. That expands to each element as a separate, properly quoted word. Any other variation — unquoted, or using a star instead of an at — will break the moment an element contains a space, and it will break silently. Learn the correct form as a single unit and always type it that way. Case is the other one, and it is bash's cleaner alternative to a long chain of elif tests when you are dispatching on a value. Each branch ends with double semicolons, and the star branch at the bottom catches everything else, which is where your usage message goes. The thing that makes case genuinely more powerful than it first looks is that the patterns are globs, not literal strings. So you can match star dot log, or prod dash star, or use a vertical bar to accept several spellings of the same option. That is why almost every init script and command-line dispatcher you will read is built on case.

Here is the lesson assembled into a health checker you could genuinely deploy. It walks a list of servers, checks whether nginx is active on each one over SSH, and reports. Notice several deliberate choices. The servers live in an array rather than a space-separated string, so a hostname with an odd character cannot break the loop. The loop quotes the array expansion correctly. Failures are collected into a second array rather than exiting on the first one — that matters, because if three servers are down you want to know about all three, not just the first. The connect timeout means one unreachable host cannot hang the whole check forever. Double parentheses give you arithmetic context, where you write a normal double-equals and less-than instead of the dash e q operators, which is much more readable. And the ending is the important part: if anything failed, it dies with a non-zero exit code listing exactly which hosts. That is what makes this script useful to automation rather than just to a human reading the screen — cron will email you, and CI will fail the pipeline. Next lesson we make scripts like this genuinely robust, with set dash e u o pipefail explained properly, traps for cleanup, and debugging techniques.
bash-scripting-advanced: This one line prevents more damage than everything else in this lesson combined, so let us understand why each piece is there. By default, bash carries on after a command fails. It prints the error and runs the next line anyway. Look at the first example and sit with how bad that is: the cd fails because the directory does not exist, so you are still in whatever directory you were in before, and then the rm dash r f runs there instead. That exact pattern has destroyed real production machines. Dash e stops the script at the first failure. Dash u makes an unset variable an error rather than an empty string. Remember the rm dash r f dollar DIR warning from the very first part of this course — with dash u, a misspelled variable name is caught immediately and named, instead of quietly expanding to nothing. It turns your worst class of bug into a clear error message. And pipefail fixes something genuinely surprising: normally a pipeline's exit code is only the last command's, so if the first stage fails but the last one succeeds, bash reports success. Your script thinks everything worked. With pipefail, any failing stage fails the pipeline. Put these three on line two of every script you write. There is essentially no downside, and one day it will stop a disaster.

Now the honest caveats, because dash e has a reputation for surprising people and you should know its limits rather than trusting it blindly. It deliberately does not trigger when a command's failure is being tested. Inside an if condition, inside a while, or on either side of the double ampersand and double pipe operators, a non-zero exit is a normal part of the logic, so dash e stays quiet. That is correct behaviour — you would not want grep failing to find something to kill your script when you are explicitly asking whether it found it. But it has a consequence worth knowing: if a function is called in a condition, dash e is disabled for that function's entire body, including commands deep inside it. So a function you thought was protected is not. The practical conclusion is this: treat dash e as a safety net for the failures you did not anticipate, not as your error handling strategy. Where you expect a command might fail, handle it explicitly with an if or a die. And where a failure genuinely does not matter, say so out loud by appending or-true, so that the next reader can see the decision was deliberate rather than an oversight. Explicitness costs one line and removes all ambiguity.

Trap registers a command to run when your script receives a signal or exits, and the EXIT trap in particular is one of the most useful things in shell scripting. It fires on every exit path — a normal finish, an error under dash e, or the user pressing Control C. That guarantee is what makes it valuable. Consider the standard pattern at the top of this slide. You create a temporary directory with mktemp dash d, and immediately register a trap to delete it on exit. From that moment you can work freely, and no matter how the script ends, the temporary directory is cleaned up. Compare that with putting a delete at the bottom of the script, which does not run if the script fails in the middle, and over months you accumulate hundreds of abandoned directories filling up your disk. The habit to build is writing the trap on the very next line after creating the thing it cleans up, so the two can never drift apart. You can also trap ERR to report which line failed, and trap INT and TERM to handle interruption gracefully. The lock file example at the bottom is a genuinely useful one: it stops two copies of a cron job running at once, and because the cleanup is in a trap, a crashed run cannot leave a stale lock that blocks every future run.

When a script misbehaves, you have better options than adding echo statements everywhere. Bash dash n checks the syntax without running anything, which is worth doing before you execute something destructive. Bash dash x is the real workhorse: it prints every command as it executes, and crucially it prints them after all expansion has happened, so you see the actual values rather than the variable names. Most shell bugs are a variable containing something you did not expect, and dash x shows you that immediately. If the trace is hard to follow, set the PS4 variable to include the source file and line number, and suddenly every traced line tells you exactly where it came from. You can also turn tracing on and off around a specific section with set dash x and set plus x, which keeps the output manageable in a long script. A small but genuinely useful habit: when printing a variable for debugging, wrap it in brackets. An empty variable and one containing three spaces look identical otherwise, and that distinction is often the entire bug. And the highest-value item on this slide is the last one. ShellCheck is a static analyser for shell scripts, it is free, and it catches unquoted variables, misused test operators and dozens of other real bugs before you ship them. Run it on everything.

Let us close Part Four with the template worth keeping, because every good script you will write starts from roughly this shape. The safety header is on line two. IFS is set to just newline and tab, which narrows word splitting and removes another class of surprise. SCRIPT underscore DIR resolves the directory the script itself lives in, which matters because a script often needs to find files next to it, and it cannot rely on the current working directory — remember cron runs it from somewhere else entirely. A temporary directory with its cleanup trap, registered immediately. The log, die and usage helpers from the previous lesson. Then getopts, which parses real command-line flags for you, so your script accepts dash v the same way every other Unix tool does, rather than you hand-inspecting dollar one. The shift at the end moves past the parsed options so the remaining positional arguments line up as you expect. Then the guard clause, and only then the actual work. Save this somewhere you can copy it from. The whole point is that starting from this costs you nothing, while adding all of it to a script that has already grown to three hundred lines is a genuinely tedious afternoon. Next we leave scripting and go to networking and SSH.
bash-scripting-basics: A shell script is nothing more mysterious than the commands you would have typed, saved in a file so you can run them again. That is genuinely the whole concept, and if you can use the terminal you can already write scripts. The first line is the shebang — a hash, an exclamation mark, and a path — and it is not a comment even though it looks like one. When you execute the file, the kernel reads those first two characters and uses the path that follows to decide which interpreter should run the rest. Write env bash rather than bin bash, because bash is not in slash bin on every system, notably not on some BSDs or on macOS with a newer bash installed by Homebrew, and env finds it wherever it lives. Below that, the script does what you would do by hand: take an argument, compute a destination filename using today's date, make the archive, print what happened. Notice every variable is wrapped in double quotes, which the next slide explains and which is the single most important habit in shell scripting. And remember from the permissions lesson: a new file is not executable, so chmod plus x before you can run it.

If you remember one rule from this entire lesson, make it this one: put double quotes around every variable, every single time. Here is why. When the shell substitutes a variable, it then splits the result on spaces and expands any glob characters in it. So a variable holding a filename with a space in it turns into two separate arguments, and your command operates on two files that do not exist while the real one sits untouched. Worse, if the value happens to contain a star, the shell expands it against the directory, which can turn a targeted command into one that hits everything. Quoting prevents all of this by making the value a single argument, exactly as intended. Single quotes are the strictest: nothing inside them is expanded at all, which is what you want for regex patterns as we saw earlier. Double quotes allow variable and command substitution while still preventing word splitting, which is why they are the everyday default. And for forwarding arguments to another command, use dollar at inside double quotes — that expands to each argument separately and correctly quoted. Bare dollar at loses the quoting, and quoted dollar star mashes everything into one string. Quoted dollar at is the correct one, essentially always.

Scripts take arguments through numbered variables: dollar one is the first, dollar two the second, and so on, while dollar hash tells you how many were supplied and dollar zero is the script's own name, which is handy for usage messages. Start every script with a guard clause that checks it received what it needs and exits with a helpful message otherwise. Two details in that check are worth doing properly. Send the message to standard error using greater-than ampersand two, because it is a diagnostic rather than output, and anyone piping your script deserves clean data. And exit with one, not zero, so that whatever called your script knows it failed. Bash also has two parameter expansions that replace a surprising amount of boilerplate. Colon dash supplies a default value when the variable is unset or empty, so you can write a fallback in a single line. Colon question mark does the opposite: it aborts with your error message if the variable is missing, which is a whole validation if-statement compressed into the place you use the variable. Learn both. They make scripts noticeably shorter and, more importantly, they put the check right where the value is used rather than twenty lines away.

Exit codes are how programs report success or failure to whatever ran them, and getting this right is what separates a script that automates something from a script that merely prints things. The convention is that zero means success and any non-zero value means failure, which is the opposite of truthiness in most programming languages and does trip people up. Dollar question mark holds the exit code of the last command, so you can inspect it. The double ampersand and double pipe operators build on this: double ampersand runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded, double pipe only if it failed. That is how you chain steps that depend on each other, and it is much cleaner than nesting if-statements. Now the point that actually matters in practice. Everything automated reads your exit code. Your CI pipeline decides whether the build passed by looking at it. Cron decides whether to email you. Systemd's restart on failure setting depends on it entirely. So a script that catches its own errors, prints a nice red message, and then exits zero anyway is completely invisible to automation — as far as the system is concerned it succeeded. If your script fails, it must exit non-zero. Otherwise, nothing downstream will ever notice.

Let us put the whole lesson into one script that you would be happy to find on a server. Read it top to bottom and notice the shape, because the shape is the lesson. The shebang uses env. Set dash e u o pipefail is on line two, which we cover properly next time but which you should include in everything from now on. Then a usage function and a guard clause, so the script refuses to start unless it has what it needs, and it exits with two by convention for a usage error. Then the inputs, with a sensible default for the optional second argument. Then validation of the actual environment — does the source directory really exist — before anything is created or written. Only after all of that does the real work happen. Every single variable is in double quotes. Nothing is hardcoded that could be a variable. And at the end it tells you exactly what it produced and how big it is, because a script that works silently is a script you cannot trust. That structure — guards first, work second, report last — is the pattern to reuse. Next lesson adds loops and functions, and after that we make scripts genuinely robust.
capstone-toolkit: For the capstone you are going to build a small ops toolkit, and deliberately nothing in it is new. Every technique comes from a lesson you have already done; the work here is wiring them together into something that runs by itself and that you would genuinely be willing to depend on. Three tools. A log analyser that uses grep, regex and awk to turn a day of raw logs into a short report you can read in thirty seconds. A health checker that uses SSH and curl across a list of hosts and tells you what is broken. And a backup script that uses tar, rsync and flock to make dated offsite archives safely. Plus a shared library holding the log, die and require helpers, so the boilerplate is written once. Notice the structure follows the philosophy from the very first lesson: three small programs that each do one thing well, rather than one large script with a mode flag. That means you can run any of them by hand, test them independently, and combine them freely. And the last step is what elevates it from a folder of scripts to something real: installing them as systemd timers so they run on schedule, log to the journal, and tell you when they fail.

The log analyser is Part Three assembled into something useful. It answers four questions about a day of traffic. Which status codes came back, and how many of each — that is awk using an associative array as a group-by on the status column, exactly the technique from the awk lesson. Which client IPs hit us most — the counting idiom, sort into uniq dash c into sort dash r n, which you should now recognize instantly. Which URLs are returning server errors — a regex matching five hundred codes, then the same counting idiom on the path field, and this one is genuinely valuable because it turns thousands of error lines into a ranked list of which endpoints are actually broken. And total bandwidth, which is awk summing a column. Four questions, about fifteen lines, no dependencies beyond what is on every Linux box. Notice the top of the script: the safety header, sourcing the shared library relative to the script's own location rather than the working directory, and validating the argument with the colon-question-mark expansion before doing anything. That is the template from Part Four, and from here on every tool starts the same way.

The health checker combines Parts Two, Four and Five. It reads a list of hosts using the correct while-read incantation, skipping blank lines and comments with a glob match inside double brackets — so the hosts file can be documented. For each host it checks three layers outward, in order, exactly as the networking lesson recommended. Can I reach it over SSH at all? Is the service actually running, checked with systemctl? And does the application respond on its health endpoint? Because each check stops on first failure with continue, the report tells you not just that a host is unhealthy but at which layer it broke, and that distinction is what makes the output actionable rather than merely alarming. Two flags carry real weight here. ConnectTimeout stops one dead host hanging the entire run. And BatchMode equals yes is genuinely essential for anything scheduled: without it, if key authentication fails, SSH falls back to prompting for a password, and in cron there is no terminal, so the job hangs forever holding a lock. With BatchMode it fails immediately and reports honestly. Failures are collected and reported at the end, and the script exits non-zero, so the scheduler notices.

The backup script is where the safety habits from across the course come together, and it is worth reading as a checklist of them. Require checks the dependencies exist before doing anything, so it fails immediately with a clear message rather than halfway through. Flock takes an exclusive lock and exits quietly if another run is in progress, which prevents the overlap problem from the cron lesson. Mktemp creates a temporary directory, and the trap on the very next line guarantees it is removed no matter how the script ends — success, error under dash e, or Control C. The directory is validated before anything is created. The archive is built with a dated name and unwanted files excluded. Rsync ships it with dash dash partial so a dropped connection can resume rather than restarting. And it logs what it did, with the size, so the journal has a record you can check. Every one of those is a habit from an earlier lesson, and together they make the difference between a script that usually works and one you can leave running unattended for a year. And I will say it once more because it is the single most ignored piece of advice in operations: test your restores. Schedule that too.

The final step is installing the toolkit as systemd timers, and this is what turns three scripts into infrastructure. The health check runs every fifteen minutes with a randomized delay so it does not stampede; the backup runs nightly and persistently, so a missed run is caught up rather than skipped forever. Because the scripts exit non-zero on failure and log to the journal, systemd records every run and you can review the history with journalctl. Keep the whole toolkit in git alongside your dotfiles, so a new machine is one clone and one install script away from being fully monitored. And now step back and look at what you can actually do. Twenty-six lessons ago the terminal was a black window. You can now navigate and reason about a filesystem, diagnose permissions, find and stop a runaway process, manage services with systemd, pull answers out of logs with grep and awk and regex, write shell scripts that fail safely and clean up after themselves, move around and between machines over SSH, schedule work so it happens without you, and explain exactly what a container is made of. That last one is the door to your next course. Go and learn Docker and Kubernetes now — and because of everything here, none of it will be magic. Well done.
cron-scheduled-tasks: Cron runs commands on a schedule, and the schedule is five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. Everyone finds them fiddly at first, and the trick that helps is reading them right to left, from the coarsest unit to the finest — most jobs only need the last two fields set and stars everywhere else. A star means every value, and the slash notation means a step, so star slash fifteen in the minute field means every fifteen minutes. That trips people up regularly: it does not mean at quarter past, it means every fifteen. Edit your crontab with crontab dash e rather than editing files directly, because that validates the syntax before installing it and reloads cron for you. And note that your crontab and root's crontab are entirely separate — sudo crontab dash e edits a different file, which is a common source of a job that seems to have vanished. My honest recommendation: use crontab dot guru to check any expression before you commit to it. Cron expressions are exactly the kind of thing that looks obviously right and runs at the wrong time, and you will not find out until three in the morning some day next week.

Here is the problem you will absolutely hit, so let us prevent it rather than let you discover it. Your script works perfectly when you run it, and does nothing at all from cron. The cause is essentially always the environment. Cron does not run your shell configuration — no bashrc, no aliases, no virtual environment activation. It gives the job a minimal PATH containing usually just usr bin and bin, so any command installed anywhere else is simply not found. The working directory is your home, not wherever the script lives, so relative paths point somewhere unexpected. This is the non-interactive shell behaviour we covered in Part Four, and now you see why it mattered. The fixes are straightforward. Use absolute paths for everything, including the interpreter — write the full path to python, not just python. Do not depend on PATH at all. And critically, redirect both output and errors to a log file on every cron line, because otherwise cron mails the output to a local mailbox nobody reads, and your job fails silently for weeks. If you are still stuck, the debugging trick at the bottom is excellent: schedule a job that just dumps the environment to a file, look at it, and you will see exactly what your script is actually running with.

Let us write one properly. Files in etc cron dot d are the tidy way to install system jobs, because each application gets its own file that you can deploy and remove cleanly, rather than everything piling into one shared crontab. Note that these files have an extra field for which user to run as, which the personal crontab does not. Setting PATH and SHELL at the top of the file is much cleaner than writing absolute paths on every line, and it fixes the environment problem from the previous slide in one place. MAILTO sends failures to a real address if your machine can send mail. Now the failure mode people do not anticipate: overlap. Suppose you schedule a backup hourly, and one day the data grows enough that it takes seventy minutes. Cron does not know or care that the previous run is still going — it starts another one. Now two backups are competing for the same disk, each making the other slower, and by the afternoon you have a dozen overlapping jobs and a server on its knees. Flock prevents this with a lock file: the second run finds the lock held and exits immediately. Combine it with the trap from the scripting lesson so a crashed run cannot leave a stale lock behind that blocks everything afterwards.

Systemd timers are the modern alternative to cron, and while cron is simpler for a one-line job, timers are genuinely better for anything that matters. A timer is two files: a service unit describing what to run, exactly like the units from the systemd lesson, and a timer unit describing when. The advantages are concrete. Logging is automatic — the output goes to the journal, so journalctl dash u backup gives you a full history with timestamps, and you do not have to remember the redirect that cron requires. Persistent equals true handles a case cron simply cannot: if the machine was powered off when the job was due, cron skips it silently and forever, whereas a persistent timer notices on the next boot and runs it. For a laptop or any machine that is not always on, that difference matters a great deal. RandomizedDelaySec spreads the load, which stops a hundred servers all hitting your backup storage at exactly three o'clock. And you get the whole systemd toolkit for free: resource limits, dependency ordering, automatic restart, and the ability to just run the service by hand to test it, without waiting for the schedule. Finally, list-timers shows every scheduled job on the machine with its next run time, which cron has no equivalent for at all.

Let us close Part Seven's first lesson with the thing that actually matters about scheduled work, which is not writing it but knowing whether it is still happening. Here is the failure that catches organizations. Everyone sets up alerts for when a job fails. Almost nobody sets up alerts for when a job stops running at all. And that second case is far more common and far worse: a machine gets rebuilt, a crontab is not migrated, a timer is not re-enabled, and the nightly backup quietly stops. Nothing fails, because nothing runs. No alert fires. Six months later you need to restore, and there is nothing there. The solution is a dead man's switch, and it inverts the logic: your job pings a monitoring service on success, and that service alerts you when an expected ping does not arrive. Now silence is what triggers the alarm, which is exactly the right way round. Several free services do this and it takes about five minutes to set up. Along with that: log with timestamps, exit non-zero on failure so the scheduler can see it, and check journalctl and list-timers periodically. And the last line on that slide is the most important sentence in this lesson: test your restores. A backup you have never restored from is not a backup, it is a hope.
filesystem-hierarchy: The first surprise coming from Windows is that there are no drive letters. There is no C drive. There is exactly one tree, and it starts at a single forward slash, which we call root. Everything on the machine hangs somewhere off that one tree. So what happens when you plug in a second hard disk? It does not become D. Instead you mount it — you attach it to a directory somewhere in the existing tree, maybe at slash mnt slash data, and from then on its contents simply appear at that path. This is genuinely more flexible than drive letters, because you can graft storage anywhere it is useful. A busy database can get its own fast disk mounted at exactly the directory the database writes to, and the software never knows or cares. Now look at the top-level directories. They can seem arbitrary and historical, and some of them honestly are, but most follow one clean idea, which the next slide is about. For now just notice: configuration in etc, users in home, logs in var, temporary junk in tmp, and installed programs in usr.

Here is the idea that turns this from trivia you memorize into a map you can reason with. The directories are separated by who writes to them and how often. Etc is configuration: small text files, edited by a human, changed rarely. That single fact is why backing up etc gives you most of a machine's personality in a few megabytes. Usr is installed software, written by the package manager — you do not hand-edit things in there, and if you find yourself doing so, you are probably fighting the system. Var is the interesting one: it holds data that varies while the machine runs. Logs, caches, mail queues, database files. It is the directory that grows, which means var is almost always the answer when a server runs out of disk at three in the morning, and slash var slash log is the first place you look. And tmp is scratch space that you should assume disappears on reboot, because on most systems it genuinely does. So the practical version: config in etc, programs in usr, growing data in var, disposable junk in tmp. Once you hold that, you can guess where an unfamiliar program put something and usually be right.

Two directories deserve their own slide because they are where the everything is a file idea becomes literal, and they surprise people. Slash proc contains no files at all. Nothing there exists on your disk. When you read slash proc slash cpuinfo, the kernel generates that text at the instant you ask and hands it to you. Read it again a second later and you may get different numbers. It is a live window into the kernel's own state, dressed up as files so that ordinary tools like cat and grep can interrogate it without needing any special interface. Every running process gets a directory in there too, named after its process ID, containing everything the kernel knows about it. Slash dev is the same trick applied to hardware. Your disk is a file there. Your terminal is a file. And slash dev slash null is the famous one: a file that discards absolutely everything written to it, which is how you throw away output you do not want to see. We will use that constantly once we get to redirection. The pattern to take away: when Linux wants to expose something, it makes it look like a file, because then every tool you already know just works on it.

Paths come in two flavours and mixing them up is the source of a great many broken scripts. An absolute path starts with a slash. It begins at the root of the tree and means exactly the same thing no matter where you are standing when you type it. A relative path does not start with a slash, and it is interpreted from your current directory — so the same relative path means different things depending on where you are. Both are useful. Relative paths are quick and natural when you are typing by hand and working inside one project. But in a script, prefer absolute paths, because a script has no idea where someone will run it from, and a relative path that worked when you tested it will silently point somewhere else when cron runs it from a different directory. That is a genuinely common bug. A few shorthands to know: a single dot is here, two dots is one level up, and a tilde is your home directory. And one more thing about hidden files — files beginning with a dot. They are not protected or secret in any way. It is purely a naming convention that tells ls not to show them by default, which is why configuration files are named that way: to keep your home directory looking tidy.

Let us make this practical, because you will regularly land on a machine you have never seen before and need to orient yourself fast. Start with df dash h. That lists every mounted filesystem with human-readable sizes, so in one line you learn what disks exist and which one is nearly full. When something is full, follow it with du dash s h on the suspect directory to find what is eating the space. Those two commands in that order are the standard drill for the most common emergency you will face, which is a server that has run out of disk because a log file grew without limit. Find searches the tree for files matching a pattern, and you will often see it written with the two-greater-than-slash-dev-slash-null incantation on the end. That is throwing away the permission denied errors you get from directories you cannot read, so the results you actually want are not buried in noise. It looks cryptic now and it will be completely clear after the redirection lesson in Part Three. And which tells you which binary actually runs when you type a command, which is how you settle the surprisingly common mystery of why the wrong version of python is starting up.
grep-basics: Grep prints the lines of its input that match a pattern. That is the entire concept, and everything else is flags. But the flags are where the productivity lives, so let us go through the ones that earn their place. Dash i ignores case, which matters more than you would think because logs are wildly inconsistent about whether they write error, Error, or ERROR. Dash n shows line numbers, essential when you are about to open the file in an editor. Dash v inverts the match, showing every line that does not match — people constantly forget this exists and write awkward workarounds instead, when they simply want to exclude noise. Dash w matches whole words only, which stops a search for cat from also matching concatenate and vacation, and that one saves real time on a large codebase. Dash r recurses through directories, dash l lists only the filenames rather than the matching lines, which is what you want when the question is which files mention this thing. And dash q prints nothing at all and just sets the exit code, which is how you use grep inside a shell script's if statement. Those nine cover almost everything you will ever need.

If you take one thing from this lesson, take this flag, because it is the difference between grep as a curiosity and grep as a serious debugging tool. The problem with plain grep is that a matching line on its own is very often not the answer. You search a build log for Traceback, you find the word Traceback, and it tells you nothing at all — because the useful information is in the thirty lines underneath it. Dash A shows lines after the match, dash B shows lines before, and dash C shows context on both sides. For stack traces you want dash A, because the exception header is the first line and the whole story follows it. For working out what caused something, you want dash B, to see what the system was doing in the moments leading up to the error. And when you do not know which, dash C three gives you a few lines each way and is a perfectly good default. This is genuinely the flag that makes grep useful in continuous integration logs, where a failing build produces thousands of lines and the actual failure is a small block buried somewhere in the middle. Search for the marker, print the block around it, and you are done.

Searching a whole project is where grep earns its keep daily, and there are two flags that turn it from frustrating into pleasant. First, exclude dir. Without it, a recursive search wades through your dot git directory, your node modules, your virtual environment — thousands of files you do not care about — and buries the handful of real results. Excluding those three makes the same search fast and readable. Second, include, which restricts the search to files matching a pattern, so you can search only Python files or only YAML. Now, a workflow worth internalizing: grep dash r l gives you just the list of filenames containing something, and that list is exactly what you feed into sed to perform a project-wide rename. Find the files, then change them. We will do precisely that in the sed and awk lesson. A practical note to close on. If you can install things, ripgrep is the same idea implemented much faster, and it automatically respects your gitignore, so the exclusions are handled for you. It is a genuinely better daily tool. But learn grep regardless, because grep is on every machine you will ever SSH into, including the minimal container at three in the morning where nothing else is installed.

Here is the use of grep that beginners never see and scripts depend on entirely: grep's exit code. Every command in Unix returns a number when it finishes, where zero conventionally means success. Grep uses this to report whether it found anything. Exit zero means it matched something, one means it matched nothing, and two means an actual error occurred, like the file not existing. Because the shell treats zero as true, grep becomes a boolean test you can put directly in an if statement, and that is the foundation of an enormous amount of automation. Your continuous integration pipeline failing the build when the log contains the word ERROR is doing exactly this. Pair it with dash q, which suppresses all output and, importantly, stops reading at the very first match — so testing whether a huge file contains something is fast, because grep does not need to read the rest. And do notice the distinction between exit one and exit two, because it matters in careful scripts. Found nothing is a normal, expected answer. Could not read the file is a failure you probably want to handle differently. A script that treats them the same will silently report all clear when it was actually unable to look.

Let us close by putting grep into the shape of a real debugging session, because the individual flags matter less than the loop you run them in. Step one: is anything actually wrong, and how much? Count the error lines. A number gives you scale immediately — three errors and thirty thousand errors are completely different situations. Step two: classify. Pipe the matching lines through cut to strip the timestamps, then that counting idiom from the last lesson, and now you have a ranked list of which kinds of error are happening and how often. Very often this alone identifies the problem, because one error type dominates everything. Step three: take the worst one and look at a single instance in full, with the stack trace after it. Step four, and this is the highest-value question in debugging: when did it start? Grep for it and take the first occurrence. A timestamp tells you what deploy, what config change, or what traffic spike lines up with the beginning of the problem, and that usually points straight at the cause. Count, classify, inspect, and date it. That loop will serve you for your whole career. Next lesson we make the patterns themselves much more powerful, with regular expressions.
links-and-editors: To understand links you need one idea underneath them, and it is a genuinely clarifying one. The file — the actual data, its size, its owner, its permissions, its timestamps — lives in a structure called an inode, and the inode has no name. Names live separately, in directories. A directory is really just a table mapping names to inode numbers. So a filename is not the file. It is a pointer to the file. Once you see that, several things that seemed strange become obvious. Why is renaming a file instant even if the file is fifty gigabytes? Because you only edited one row in a table; the data never moved. Why does the deletion command in the C library get called unlink? Because that is literally what it does — it removes a name, not data. The kernel keeps a count of how many names point at each inode, and only when that count drops to zero does the actual data get freed. And here is a consequence that will genuinely help you one day: if a process still has the file open, the data survives even after every name is gone. That is why deleting a huge log file sometimes does not give you your disk space back until you restart the service holding it open.

Now the two kinds of link, and the difference is entirely about that inode picture. A hard link is simply a second name pointing at the same inode. The two names are peers — there is no original and no copy, and nothing in the system records which one came first. Delete either and the other keeps working perfectly, because the data only disappears when the last name goes. A symbolic link, or symlink, is a completely different animal. It is a tiny file whose entire contents are a path — a signpost that says look over there. When you open it, the kernel reads the path and follows it. Because it stores a path rather than pointing at an inode, a symlink can point across to a different disk, and it can point at a directory, neither of which a hard link can do. But it can also dangle: delete what it points at and the symlink remains, now pointing at nothing, and you get a no such file error even though the link is clearly sitting right there. In practice you will use symlinks nearly all the time and hard links almost never — but knowing the difference is what lets you diagnose a dangling link instead of staring at it.

Rather than leave symlinks as theory, let me show you the three places you will genuinely meet them, because they are the same trick each time. First, version switching. The python3 command in usr bin is usually a symlink to a specific version like python3.11. Upgrading the system python means moving one link, not reinstalling anything. Second, enabling and disabling features. Nginx and many other services use a pair of directories called sites-available and sites-enabled, where enabling a site means creating a symlink from one to the other, and disabling it means deleting that link. Your actual configuration file never moves and never gets edited. Third, and this is the elegant one: zero-downtime deployment. You keep a symlink called current pointing at a dated release directory. To deploy, you build the entire new release alongside the old one, taking as long as you like, and then you move the symlink. Because repointing a link is a single atomic operation, there is no instant where the site is half-updated, and rolling back is just pointing the link at yesterday's directory. Some very sophisticated-sounding infrastructure is, underneath, exactly this.

You will need to edit a file on a machine with no graphical interface, and there are two editors you should know. Nano is the one you can use right now with no training at all. You open a file, you type, the arrow keys move the cursor, and it behaves the way every text box you have ever used behaves. The shortcuts are printed along the bottom of the screen, so there is nothing to memorize — the only thing to know is that the caret symbol means Control, so caret X displayed at the bottom means press Control X to exit. Save is Control O, which is a slightly odd choice for something called write out, and exit is Control X. And let me say this plainly, because a certain kind of person online will tell you otherwise: if nano is installed, use nano. There is no shame in it. The editor is not the job. Plenty of extremely capable engineers edit config files in nano their entire careers, and the work is exactly as good. The reason to learn any vim at all is not superiority — it is that vim is installed absolutely everywhere, including minimal containers and rescue systems where nano simply is not present.

And now vim, taught as a survival skill rather than a religion. The famous confusion, the reason people joke about being trapped in vim forever, is one design decision: vim starts in normal mode, where the letter keys are commands rather than text. So you open a file, type hello expecting to see hello, and instead the cursor jumps around and things get deleted, because h and e and l are all commands. Here is the whole survival kit. Press i to enter insert mode, and now you can type normally like any other editor. Press Escape to leave insert mode and go back to normal mode. If you are ever lost or confused, press Escape — it always returns you to a known state, and pressing it when you are already there does nothing at all, so it is completely safe to mash. Then colon w writes the file, colon q quits, and colon w q does both. The most important one on this slide is colon q exclamation mark, which quits and throws away every change you made. That is your escape hatch. If you have accidentally mangled a config file on a production server, colon q exclamation gets you out with the file untouched. Learn those five things and vim can never trap you again.
linux-in-containers-preview: Here is the sentence this entire course has been building toward. There is no such thing as a container. The Linux kernel has no container object, no container system call, nothing named container anywhere in it. What we call a container is an ordinary Linux process that the kernel has been asked to lie to — a process that has been given a restricted view of the system using several independent kernel features that existed long before Docker. You can verify this yourself in about ten seconds. Start nginx in a container, then run ps on the host, and there it is, sitting in the host's process list alongside everything else, with a normal process ID. It is not inside anything. It is right there. This is also precisely why containers differ so much from virtual machines. A VM emulates hardware and boots an entire separate kernel, which is why it takes a minute to start and consumes hundreds of megabytes doing nothing. A container is just a process sharing your existing kernel, which is why it starts in milliseconds and costs almost nothing when idle. Everything else about Docker — images, registries, compose files — is tooling built around this one idea. The idea itself is what the next few slides unpack.

Namespaces are the first half of the trick, and they control what a process can see. There are seven kinds, each independent of the others, and each one virtualizes a different part of the system. The PID namespace gives the process its own process tree, so inside the container it believes it is process one — the init process — while on the host it is process four one two seven. Same process, two different numbers, depending on who is asking. The mount namespace gives it its own filesystem tree, which is how a container sees a completely different root directory from yours. The network namespace gives it its own interfaces, IP addresses and ports, which is why two containers can both bind port eighty without conflicting. The user namespace maps user IDs, so root inside the container need not be root outside it — which is a major security property. And crucially, these are independent. You can opt out of any of them individually, which is exactly what docker run with network host does: everything else is isolated, but it shares the host's network. You can even create namespaces by hand with unshare and watch it work, no Docker involved. Do try it — running that command and seeing your shell believe it is PID one makes the whole concept click permanently.

If namespaces control what a process can see, control groups — cgroups — control what it can use. They meter and cap resources: memory, CPU time, disk bandwidth, and the number of processes it may create. This is the half that makes shared infrastructure viable, because without it a single misbehaving container could consume all the memory on a node and take down everything else running there. And as you would now expect on Linux, cgroups are exposed as files. You can look under slash sys slash fs slash cgroup and read the current limits and usage of anything running, with cat. When you write memory equals five twelve megabytes in a Docker command, that is all that ultimately happens — a number gets written into a file. Now, one very practical thing to take away, because you will meet it. If a container exceeds its memory limit, the kernel kills it, and the exit code is one thirty seven. That number is not arbitrary: it is one twenty eight plus nine, and nine is SIGKILL. So exit code one thirty seven means the out-of-memory killer got it. When a container keeps dying with one thirty seven and no error in its own logs, stop looking for a bug in the application — either raise the memory limit or find the leak.

The last piece is the filesystem. The old Unix chroot call changed a process's root directory, and the mount namespace is a far more thorough version of that idea: a container gets its own complete filesystem tree, which is why it can run Alpine's userland while your host is Ubuntu. The clever part is how that filesystem is assembled. An image is built from stacked read-only layers, one per Dockerfile instruction, combined by a union filesystem so they appear as a single tree. Layers are content-addressed and shared, so if ten images all build on Debian slim, that base is stored once on your disk and downloaded once. That is why images are far smaller in practice than their stated sizes suggest. Now the practical consequence, and this is the most useful thing on the slide. Changing any layer invalidates every layer above it, so Dockerfile ordering has a large effect on build times. Copy your dependency file and install dependencies before copying your source code. Then a change to your code only rebuilds the last layer, and the slow dependency install stays cached. Do it the other way round and every one-line change reinstalls everything. And note the writable layer at the top: it is discarded when the container is removed, which is exactly why persistent data must live in a volume.

Let us put the whole course into one picture. Here is a single ordinary docker run command, and underneath it, everything the system actually does — with the part of this course that taught you each piece. It creates namespaces so the process has its own process tree, network and filesystem: that is Parts One and Two. It sets up a cgroup with a memory ceiling: resource limits, Part Two. It mounts the image layers as the root filesystem: Part One. It creates a virtual network interface pair and a NAT rule to forward port eight thousand eighty to eighty inside: Part Five. It drops privileges to the image's configured user: Part Two again. It executes nginx as PID one inside that namespace: processes. And it captures standard output and standard error as the container's log stream: Part Three. There is not one item on that list that is Docker-specific. Every single one is a Linux feature you now understand, and Docker's genuine contribution is packaging them into a command you can type in one line, plus a format for shipping filesystems around. Go and prove it to yourself: docker exec into a running container and run ps and ls, and you will see an ordinary Linux system. That is the payoff, and it is why this course came before the Docker one.
navigating-files: Four ways to read a file, and choosing the right one is most of the skill. Cat dumps the whole thing to your screen at once, which is perfect for a short config file and a disaster for a two gigabyte log — you will be scrolling for a very long time. Less is the pager: it shows one screen at a time, you move with the arrow keys, slash searches inside it, and q quits. When in doubt, use less. Head and tail show you the beginning and the end, and for logs the end is almost always what you want, because logs append. But the one I want you to really take away is tail dash f. The f stands for follow, and it means the command does not exit — it sits there and prints new lines as they are written to the file. This is the single most useful habit in this whole lesson. You open tail dash f on the application log in one terminal, then go and reproduce the bug in another, and you watch the error appear in real time as it happens. That is how debugging on a server actually feels, and it beats guessing every time.

Globs are the wildcard patterns that let you act on many files at once, and there is one thing about them you must internalize: the shell expands them before the command ever runs. When you type rm star dot log, the rm program never sees a star. The shell first looks in the directory, finds every matching filename, and hands rm the complete list. Rm just receives a pile of filenames and deletes them. This matters enormously for safety, and it gives you a free safety drill that I want you to adopt permanently. Before you run a destructive command with a glob, run the exact same pattern with ls first. The shell expands it identically, so what ls prints is precisely the list that rm would have received. Look at it. If it is what you expected, press up-arrow, change ls to rm, and run it. That one habit will save you from the worst day of your career. And note the last line on this slide: a bare star does not match dotfiles. So a star will not catch your hidden configuration files, which is usually a mercy but occasionally a nasty surprise when you are copying a directory and wonder why the config did not come along.

Copy, move, and make directory — the everyday verbs. Cp copies, and for a directory you need dash r for recursive, otherwise it refuses. Mv both renames and moves, because to Linux those are the same operation: a rename is just moving a file to a new name in the same directory. Mkdir makes directories, and dash p is the flag you want almost always, because it creates any missing parent directories and does not error if the thing already exists. That makes it idempotent, meaning safe to run repeatedly, which is exactly what you want in a script. Now the sharp edge, and it is genuinely sharp. Both cp and mv will overwrite an existing file silently. No prompt, no warning, no undo, no trash can. If you copy over an important file, it is simply gone. You can pass dash i to make them ask first, and many people alias cp and mv to always include it. That is a reasonable thing to do on your own machine, though be aware that if you get used to the prompt, you will be missing it on a server where the alias is not set — so the habit of thinking before you press enter is still the real protection.

This one gets its own slide because it deserves the respect. Rm deletes, and it deletes permanently. There is no trash can, no recycle bin, no undo, no control z. The bytes are unlinked and gone. Dash r makes it recursive so it can delete directories, and dash f forces it to never ask, and the combination dash r f is simultaneously the most useful and most dangerous thing in this course. Two specific ways people destroy machines with it, so you can recognize the shape. The first is a stray space. You mean to type rm dash r f dot slash old, but a space slips in after the slash, and now you have told it to delete the root of the filesystem and also a directory called old. The second is more common in scripts: you write rm dash r f dollar-DIR slash, and if that variable is empty or misspelled, it expands to nothing, and your command becomes rm dash r f slash. That has taken down real production systems more than once. The protection is the same drill as the globs: run ls with the exact path first, look at what comes back, and only then change ls to rm. Slow is fine. Gone is forever.

Let us put the lesson together the way you will actually use it. Someone says the app is broken. Here is a sixty-second triage using only what you now know. Change into the application's log directory. Run ls dash l a t — long format, all files, sorted by modification time — so the most recently touched file is right at the top, and that is almost always the one that matters. Tail the last hundred lines of the error log to see what just happened. Then open tail dash f on it and go reproduce the problem, watching the errors appear live. That is a genuinely effective workflow and it is entirely built from this one lesson. The last line on the slide is a preview: piping into grep to filter for just the lines you care about. That is Part Three, and it is where this goes from survivable to fast. But notice you already have the shape of the thing. Next lesson is permissions — which is the other half of why things break on servers, because roughly half of all permission denied mysteries come down to a single wrong digit in a chmod.
networking-basics: Two numbers get a packet to the right place. The IP address identifies the machine, and the port identifies which program on that machine should receive it. That is the whole model, and holding it clearly explains most of what follows. Some addresses are worth recognizing on sight. One-two-seven dot zero dot zero dot one is localhost, meaning this machine and only this machine — traffic to it never leaves the box. The ten-dot, one-seventy-two-dot-sixteen-through-thirty-one, and one-ninety-two-dot-one-sixty-eight ranges are private, used inside home networks and cloud VPCs, and not routable on the public internet. And zero dot zero dot zero dot zero is not really an address at all; when a server binds to it, it means listen on every interface I have. Which brings us to the single most common networking confusion in deployment, so let us name it now. If a service binds to one-two-seven dot zero dot zero dot one, it will work perfectly when you test it from the same machine and refuse every connection from anywhere else. Works locally but refused remotely is almost always this. The fix is binding to zero dot zero dot zero dot zero — and then, because you have just exposed it to the world, making sure your firewall is doing its job.

Here is the diagnostic sequence, and the value is entirely in doing it in order, because each step eliminates one layer. Step one: is the service even listening? Run ss with dash t l n p — TCP, listening, numeric so it does not waste time resolving names, and p to show which process owns each port. If your service is not in that list, nothing else matters; the problem is the service, not the network. Step two: can you connect from the same machine, with curl to localhost? If that works but remote does not, you have learned something precise — the service is fine, so the problem is either the bind address or a firewall. Step three: connect from another machine. Netcat with dash z v is the sharpest tool here, and the way it fails tells you which problem you have. An instant connection refused means nothing is listening on that port, or the port is closed. A long hang followed by a timeout means a firewall is silently dropping your packets, which is what firewalls are configured to do. That distinction between fast refusal and slow silence is genuinely diagnostic and will save you a lot of guessing. And one caveat on ping: many cloud providers block ICMP by default, so a failed ping does not prove the host is down.

DNS turns names into addresses, and it is the layer that produces the most it worked yesterday incidents, so it earns a slide. Dig is the tool; add plus short when you just want the answer and not the full record detail. The most useful trick with dig is pointing it at a specific resolver with the at sign. Ask your own machine, then ask Google's public resolver, and compare. If they differ, you have distinguished two very different problems: your local or corporate resolver has a stale cached answer, versus the change genuinely has not propagated yet. Do check etc hosts too, because entries there are consulted before DNS and override it completely. A line someone added for local testing months ago and forgot about is a classic source of an hour of confusion, especially when one person on a team can reach a host and nobody else can. And the concept to hold on to is TTL, time to live: every DNS record carries a duration telling resolvers how long they may cache it. When you update a record and nothing changes, the answer is usually just that the old value is still cached somewhere and you need to wait out the TTL. Resist the urge to change things again during that window; you will only confuse yourself.

Curl is how you talk to HTTP from the command line and you will use it constantly, so learn the handful of flags that matter. Dash i shows the response headers along with the body, which is how you check status codes and content types. Dash capital I fetches only the headers. Dash capital L follows redirects, and its absence explains a lot of confusion, because without it curl shows you the redirect response rather than the page you expected. Dash s silences the progress meter so output is clean in a pipeline. Now the flag that matters most and is most often missed: dash f. By default, curl considers itself successful if it managed to talk to the server at all — so a five hundred error still exits zero, and your script happily continues as if everything worked. Dash f makes an HTTP error status produce a non-zero exit code. If you are using curl in a script or a health check, you need it. Pair it with dash s capital S, which stays quiet but still prints actual errors, and you have the right combination for automation. Two extras worth knowing: piping into jq pretty-prints and queries JSON, and dash w with the timing variables turns curl into a lightweight performance probe that tells you the status code and how long the request took.

Let us close with the discipline rather than more commands, because knowing the tools matters far less than using them in a sensible order. When something cannot reach something else, work outward from the service, one layer at a time, and let each result eliminate a cause. Is the process listening, and on which address? Does it answer on localhost? Can another machine open a TCP connection to the port? Does the name resolve to the address you expect? Does the full HTTPS request work end to end? Five checks, each one narrowing the possibilities, and you will find the fault in about two minutes. Compare that with the common alternative, which is changing firewall rules and restarting things hopefully until something works — that sometimes fixes the symptom while leaving you with no idea what was wrong, and often leaves the machine less secure than it was. One thing that catches people repeatedly on cloud infrastructure: there are two firewalls, not one. The operating system has its own, and the cloud provider has a separate security group or network ACL sitting in front of the machine entirely. You can open a port perfectly in the OS and still be blocked upstream, so remember to check both. Next lesson: SSH properly, which is how you get onto these machines in the first place.
package-managers: A package manager installs software along with everything it depends on, from a curated repository, with cryptographic signatures verifying it came from who it claims. That is a great deal better than downloading a binary from a website and hoping. The commands differ by distribution but the concepts map one to one, so learning one teaches you all of them. The distinction to get right immediately is update versus upgrade, because the names are genuinely misleading. Apt update does not update any software at all — it refreshes the local catalogue of what versions are available. Apt upgrade is what actually installs newer versions. So you always run update first, then upgrade; running upgrade alone works from a stale catalogue and may install nothing or an old version. On Fedora, dnf refreshes automatically, which is arguably a better design. Two lookups worth knowing for when you inherit a machine and find a mystery file: dpkg dash capital S on Debian systems, and rpm dash q f on Red Hat ones, both answer which package installed this file. That is often how you work out what a previous administrator set up and whether you can safely remove it.

The real work a package manager does is dependency resolution. You ask for nginx and it works out the full set of libraries and supporting packages needed, in compatible versions, and installs them together. That is a genuinely hard problem and it is why you should use the package manager rather than assembling software by hand. But do read what it proposes before confirming. The line that matters most is the one listing packages to be removed. Occasionally, resolving a conflict means the manager wants to uninstall something important, and on a server that can be a very unpleasant surprise. Ten seconds of reading prevents it. Dash y answers yes automatically, and it is necessary in scripts and Dockerfiles because there is no terminal there to type into — but it does mean you have given up your chance to look, so reserve it for contexts where you have already tested the command. The recommends flag is worth knowing about. Debian packages can suggest additional packages that are nice to have but not required, and by default those get installed too. In a container, where every megabyte is shipped over the network on every deploy, no-install-recommends is standard practice and can genuinely halve a layer.

Packages come from repositories listed in the sources files, and every package is cryptographically signed. Apt verifies each signature against the keys you have installed and refuses anything that fails, which is what protects you from a compromised mirror serving a modified package. Adding a third-party repository is common — Docker, Node, Postgres all distribute this way — and the modern approach puts the key in its own file and binds it to that specific repository with the signed-by option, so a key you added for one publisher cannot be used to vouch for packages from another. Older instructions using apt-key are deprecated precisely because they added keys globally. But understand what you are agreeing to. Adding a repository means that whenever you run apt upgrade, that publisher can install software on your machine as root, automatically, without further prompting. That is a substantial amount of trust. Add few repositories and only ones you genuinely trust. And this is a good moment to mention those install instructions that say pipe curl into sudo bash. They bypass this entire verification system, and you are executing a script you have not read with root privileges. If you must, download it first, read it, then run it.

This slide is the bridge to your next course, and it explains a practice that looks obsessive until you understand the reasons. Container images are built from a base image, and the sizes vary enormously — a full Ubuntu is around eighty megabytes, Debian slim under thirty, Alpine about seven, and a distroless image around two with no shell in it at all. Why does anyone care? Three reasons. Speed: that image is pulled over the network on every deploy and onto every node, so size multiplies out quickly. Cost: registry storage and bandwidth are real. But the most important is security. Every package installed in that image is code, and code has vulnerabilities. A full distribution image ships hundreds of packages you never use, and each one can generate a security alert you must assess and patch. A minimal image simply does not contain them, so the alerts never arrive. Now the technical detail on this slide that catches everyone. Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer, and layers are stacked, never modified. So deleting files in a later RUN does not shrink the earlier layer — the data is still in the image, just hidden. That is why the install and the cleanup must be chained into one RUN command.

Sometimes the package manager does not have what you need, or has a version too old to use, so let us cover doing it properly. For language libraries, use that language's own package manager, scoped to the project. A Python virtual environment or a local node modules directory keeps each project's dependencies separate, so two projects needing different versions of the same library coexist happily. The one thing not to do, and I want to be emphatic, is sudo pip install. That writes into the system Python directories which the OS package manager also owns and tracks, and the two will fight. You end up with a broken system Python, and on distributions where system tools are written in Python — which is most of them — that can break your package manager itself, which is a genuinely bad afternoon. For a standalone binary from a project's release page, download it, verify its checksum, and install it into slash usr slash local slash bin. That directory exists precisely for locally installed software and the package manager will not touch it. But do remember the trade you have made: nothing will ever update that binary for you. It is now your responsibility to watch for security releases, which is a real reason to prefer packaged software whenever a package exists.
permissions-ownership: Everything about permissions starts with being able to read this one line, so let us decode it carefully. Run ls dash l and the first column is ten characters. The very first is not a permission at all — it is the type. A dash means an ordinary file, a d means a directory, an l means a symbolic link. Then the remaining nine split cleanly into three groups of three, and each group is the same three letters in the same order: r for read, w for write, x for execute. The first triple is what the owner may do. The second is what members of the file's group may do. The third is what everyone else — called other — may do. A dash in any position means that permission is absent. Now here is the rule that people get wrong: Linux does not add these up. It checks them in order and stops at the first match. Are you the owner? Then only the owner bits apply to you, and it does not matter how generous the group bits are. Are you in the group? Then the group bits apply. Otherwise, other. So an owner with fewer permissions than the group genuinely has less access, which surprises people the first time they meet it.

You will see permissions written as three digits constantly, so let us make the arithmetic click.
