Read is worth four, write is worth two, execute is worth one, and you simply add up the ones you want. So seven is four plus two plus one, all three permissions. Six is read plus write but no execute. Five is read plus execute, no write. Four is read only. And each digit describes one group, in the same order as before: owner, group, other. That is the whole system. Honestly, four combinations cover most of your working life, so learn these as words rather than arithmetic. Seven five five is a program: the owner can edit it, everyone can run it. Six four four is an ordinary file: the owner can edit, everyone can read. Six zero zero is a secret: only the owner, nobody else, not even read. And seven zero zero is a private directory. That third one is not optional trivia. SSH will flatly refuse to use a private key if other users on the machine can read it, and the resulting error message confuses people for hours. When SSH complains your key permissions are too open, the fix is chmod six zero zero on the key. Now you know why.

This is the single most confusing corner of Linux permissions, and once it clicks, a whole category of baffling errors becomes obvious. The three letters mean different things on a directory than they do on a file. On a directory, read does not mean you can read the files inside — it means you can list the names. And execute has nothing to do with running anything; on a directory, execute means you may pass through it, enter it, reach things by name. Now consider the strange combinations, because you will meet them. A directory with read but not execute: you can run ls and see the filenames, but you cannot open a single one of them, because you cannot enter the directory to get at them. Frustrating and quite odd-looking. The reverse, execute but not read, is actually a real technique: you cannot list what is inside, but if someone tells you the exact filename you can open it. That is how people share one specific file out of a directory without exposing the whole listing. And here is the practical consequence that catches everyone: to reach a file deep in a path, you need execute on every single directory along the way. One directory in the middle missing its x bit, and the file is unreachable even though the file's own permissions look perfect.

Chown changes who owns a file, and chgrp changes the group, though chown can do both at once with the owner colon group syntax. Notice that these need sudo. You cannot give your own file away to another user, and the reason is disk quotas — if you could, you would dodge your storage limit by making all your large files belong to someone else. Only root can hand ownership around. The recursive form, chown dash R on a whole directory tree, is one you will use constantly when setting up web servers, because the web server process runs as its own user and needs to own the files it serves. Umask is the odd one. It sets the default permissions for files you create, but it works by subtraction, which is why the numbers look inverted. The usual value is zero zero two two, and those twos subtract the write bit from group and other, which is how you end up with new files at six four four and new directories at seven five five. If you set umask to zero seven seven, everything you create is private to you by default. On a shared machine handling anything sensitive, that is a very sensible line to put in your shell configuration.

Let us close with the most common permissions problem you will actually hit, which is a script that refuses to run. You write it, you type dot slash deploy dot s h, and the shell says permission denied. Here is the checklist, in order. First and almost always the answer: the execute bit is not set. A newly written file, or anything you just downloaded, is not executable by default — that is a deliberate safety property, since otherwise downloading a file would be dangerously close to running it. Chmod plus x fixes it. Second, check the very first line of the file for the shebang, that hash-bang slash bin slash bash line, which tells the kernel what interpreter to use. Without it you can get a confusing error even when the permissions are perfect. Third, remember what we just learned about directories: you need the execute bit on every directory in the path to reach the script at all. And fourth, the one that makes people question their sanity — some filesystems, very commonly slash tmp, are deliberately mounted with the noexec option, which means nothing on them can be executed no matter what chmod says. If a script runs from your home directory but not from tmp, that is your answer.
processes-job-control: Every single thing running on a Linux machine is a process with a numeric ID, and there are two tools for looking at them that answer different questions. Ps takes a snapshot: this is what was running at the instant you asked. The flags a u x are almost always what you want, and honestly most people have simply memorized ps aux as one word. Top is the opposite — a live feed that refreshes every couple of seconds, sorted by whatever is consuming the most CPU, which makes it the right tool when the question is what is making this machine slow right now. Inside top, press capital M to sort by memory and capital P for CPU, and q to quit. If htop is installed, use it; it is the same idea with colours, mouse support and a far more readable layout. The structural thing to understand is that processes form a tree, not a list. Every process records the PID of the parent that started it. Follow those links all the way up and you arrive at PID one, which is systemd, started by the kernel at boot. Everything else on the machine is a descendant of that one process. That tree matters, because killing a parent affects its children, which is the next slide.

The kill command is badly named. What it actually does is send a signal, and killing is only one of the things signals do. The default signal is SIGTERM, number fifteen, and it means please shut down cleanly. A well-written program catches it and does the right things: finishes the request it is handling, flushes its buffers to disk, closes its database connections, and exits. SIGKILL, number nine, is completely different. It is not delivered to the program at all — the kernel simply destroys the process where it stands. It cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored, and crucially, the program gets no chance to clean up. Half-written files and corrupt databases come from dash nine. So the discipline is: always send plain kill first, wait a few seconds, and only escalate to dash nine if the process genuinely will not go. And notice SIGHUP, which most long-running daemons interpret as reload your configuration without restarting — that is how you apply a config change to a web server without dropping a single connection. One last thing that will save you confusion: if a process ignores even dash nine, it is probably in D state, stuck waiting on disk or network I/O the kernel cannot interrupt. That usually means hardware trouble or a hung network mount, not a stubborn program.

Job control solves an everyday annoyance: you start something that takes twenty minutes and it occupies your terminal, and you need that terminal for something else. Here is the rescue. Press Control Z, which suspends the process — it is frozen, not killed, and the shell hands your prompt back. Then type bg, which resumes it running in the background while you carry on working. If you want it back in front of you, fg brings it to the foreground. Jobs lists what this shell is looking after, numbered, and you refer to them with a percent sign and the number. If you know in advance that something will be slow, put an ampersand at the end of the command and it starts in the background immediately. The one thing you must understand about all of this is that jobs belong to the shell that started them. They are not independent. Close the terminal, or lose your SSH connection, and the shell sends its jobs a hangup signal, and normally they die. Which is precisely the problem the next slide solves, and it is the single most useful thing in this lesson for anyone who works on remote servers.

This is the slide that will save you a genuinely bad afternoon. You SSH into a server, start a database migration that takes forty minutes, and then your wifi hiccups or your laptop goes to sleep. The connection drops, the shell on the server receives a hangup signal, and it passes that on to your migration, which dies half-finished. Nohup is the old fix: it starts a command that ignores the hangup signal, so it survives the disconnect, and its output goes to a file called nohup dot out. That works, but you have no way to get back to it — you cannot see it, interact with it, or check on it, only read the file afterwards. Tmux is the real answer, and it is worth ten minutes of your life to learn. Tmux runs a terminal on the server itself, independent of your connection. You start a named session, run whatever you like inside it, and press Control B then D to detach. Your SSH session can then die in any way it likes and the work carries on. Later, from your laptop or a completely different machine, you reattach and find your shell exactly as you left it, scrollback and all. The rule to adopt today: any long-running command on a remote server goes inside tmux. No exceptions.

Let us end with the drill for the most common question you will be asked, which is why is this server slow. Start with uptime, because it is instant and gives you the load average over one, five and fifteen minutes. The trick to reading it is comparing against your core count from nproc: a load of four on a four-core machine is fully busy but coping, while a load of forty on that same machine means work is piling up faster than it can be done. Then top to see which process is responsible. Then free dash h for memory, and look specifically at whether the machine is swapping, because a server that has started swapping to disk becomes dramatically slow in a way that looks mysterious from the outside. Check df dash h early, even though disk space sounds unrelated to slowness, because a full disk produces some of the strangest failures you will ever debug — programs that cannot write their logs, databases that refuse connections, sessions that will not save. And finally dmesg piped to tail, which shows you kernel messages. That is where you find the out-of-memory killer, the kernel's last resort: when memory runs out entirely, it picks the biggest process and destroys it to save the machine. If a service keeps disappearing with no error in its own logs, dmesg is where the explanation is waiting.
redirection-pipes: Every process starts life with three connections already open, and understanding them is what makes the rest of this lesson obvious rather than a list of symbols to memorize. Standard input, file descriptor zero, is where the process reads from. Standard output, file descriptor one, is where it writes its normal results. And standard error, file descriptor two, is where it writes error messages and warnings. Those numbers are not trivia — they appear literally in the redirection syntax, so knowing them means you can read any redirect you encounter. Now, why separate output from errors at all? Because it keeps the data clean. Imagine searching the whole filesystem for config files and saving the results. You will hit dozens of directories you are not allowed to read, and each one produces a permission denied message. If those errors went into the same stream as your results, your saved file would be a useless mixture of filenames and complaints. Because they are separate, you can send the results to a file while the errors still appear on your screen where you can see them. The reason this is not obvious to beginners is that by default both streams go to your terminal, so they look like one thing until the first time you redirect.

Now the operators. A single greater-than sends standard output to a file, and be careful because it truncates that file to nothing before the command even starts running. If you point it at an existing file, that file's contents are gone immediately, even if the command then fails. Two greater-thans appends instead, which is the safe choice whenever you are not certain. Putting a two in front redirects standard error instead, so two-greater-than error dot txt captures just the errors. The combination two-greater-than-ampersand-one is the one that looks cryptic, so let us decode it: it means send file descriptor two to wherever file descriptor one is currently going. And that word currently is why the order matters. If you write greater-than file, then two-greater-than-ampersand-one, stdout is already pointed at the file, so stderr follows it there. Write them the other way round and stderr gets pointed at the terminal, where stdout was at that moment, and only then does stdout move to the file — leaving errors on screen. Bash offers ampersand-greater-than as a shorthand for both to one place. And two-greater-than slash dev slash null throws errors away entirely, which is that incantation from the find examples earlier, now completely explicable.

And here is the payoff — the idea the whole Unix philosophy was building toward. The pipe takes the standard output of one command and makes it the standard input of the next. That one connector is what turns a collection of narrow, unremarkable tools into something that can answer almost any question. Read the first example left to right: produce the lines of the log, keep only those containing five hundred, count what is left. Three trivial programs, none of which knows the others exist, combining into how many server errors were there. The last example is a real one worth studying — it takes your shell history, extracts the command name from each line, sorts them, counts the duplicates, sorts by that count, and shows the top few. That tells you which commands you actually use most. Six tools, one line, and no one ever wrote a program to do that. Two things worth knowing. The pipe carries standard output only, so errors still reach your terminal rather than polluting the data, which is usually exactly right. And the stages all run at the same time, streaming to each other — the pipeline does not wait for one command to finish before starting the next. That is why piping a gigantic file into head returns instantly instead of reading the whole thing.

A few more pieces and you have the whole toolkit. Tee is named after a T-shaped pipe fitting, and it does exactly that: it splits the stream so the data continues down the pipeline while also being written to a file. That is how you watch a long process on screen and keep a record of it at the same time. Then the small filters you will reuse endlessly. Sort orders lines, with dash n for proper numeric ordering, dash r to reverse, and dash h to understand human sizes like five megabytes. Uniq dash c collapses duplicates and counts them, but there is a catch that trips everyone: uniq only looks at adjacent lines, so it cannot see duplicates that are scattered. That is exactly why you always see sort piped into uniq — sorting brings the duplicates together first. Cut extracts a field, tr translates characters. And xargs solves a different problem: some commands, like rm, take arguments rather than reading standard input, so a pipe alone will not work. Xargs bridges that by turning the incoming lines into arguments. One important caveat there: filenames containing spaces break the naive version, so the safe form is find with dash print zero piped into xargs with dash zero, which separates names with a null character instead.

Let us finish with real pipelines, because this is what the skill actually looks like in use. The first one answers who is hitting my server most: pull the first field from every log line, which is the IP address, sort them, count the duplicates, sort by that count descending, take the top ten. Learn that middle sequence — sort, uniq dash c, sort dash r n — as a single unit, because it is the counting idiom, and once you recognize it you will use it for log lines, error codes, usernames, filenames, everything. The others follow the same shape: filter the source, extract the interesting part, aggregate, sort, and limit. Now the most useful advice in this lesson is about how you write these. Do not compose a six-stage pipeline in your head and run it. Run the first command alone and look at the output. Add one pipe stage, run it again, look again. Keep going. At every point you can see exactly what the data looks like, so when a stage does something unexpected you know immediately which one, instead of debugging a wall of pipes at once. Build them incrementally and pipelines stop feeling clever and start feeling routine. Next lesson: grep, in proper depth.
regex-fundamentals: A regular expression is a small language for describing the shape of text rather than exact text. That distinction is the whole idea. When you search for the literal word error you are describing exact text. When you want any line containing a date, or an IP address, or a number followed by the letters M B, you are describing a shape, and regex is how you say it. Start from this: most characters simply match themselves. The letters c, a and t in a pattern match those letters. Only a small set of metacharacters are special, and learning regex is essentially learning that set. The dot is the first, and it matches any single character. Beginners routinely misuse it — if you search for three dot one four meaning the number pi, that pattern also matches three x one four, because the dot means anything. To match an actual dot you escape it with a backslash. Then square brackets define a character class, meaning exactly one character from the set inside. A dash inside gives you a range, so a to z is any lowercase letter. And a caret at the start of the brackets inverts it, so caret zero to nine means any single character that is not a digit.

Quantifiers say how many times the previous thing may repeat, and this is where regex becomes genuinely expressive. Star means zero or more. Plus means one or more. Question mark means zero or one, so it marks something optional — colou question mark r elegantly matches both the American and British spellings. Curly braces let you be exact: three in braces means exactly three times, two comma five means between two and five, and two comma with nothing after means at least two. Two warnings that will save you real debugging time. First, a quantifier applies only to the single item immediately before it, not to everything you have written so far. So a b star means an a followed by any number of b's, not any number of a b pairs. To repeat a group you need parentheses, which is the next lesson. Second, and this is the classic beginner bug: star means zero or more, so a pattern of digit-star happily matches a line with no digits at all, because zero digits satisfies it. When you mean there must be at least one, use plus. And a portability note: plain grep needs backslashes before plus and braces, which is ugly, so just use grep dash E and write them normally.

Anchors are different from everything else so far, because they do not match a character at all. They match a position. A caret means the start of the line and a dollar sign means the end, and neither consumes anything — they simply assert where you are. That is why caret followed by dollar means an empty line: start of line immediately followed by end of line, with nothing in between. Anchors are what make a pattern precise. Searching for ERROR finds it anywhere, including in the middle of a sentence in a message. Searching for ERROR dollar finds only lines that end with it. And caret plus pattern plus dollar means the line must be exactly that and nothing else, which is what you want when matching a config value rather than a mention of it. Do notice the awkward thing about the caret: outside square brackets it means start of line, and inside square brackets it means not. It is the same symbol with two completely unrelated jobs, and that catches people. The word boundary, backslash b, is the other anchor worth knowing, and it is what grep dash w uses internally. And the pipeline at the bottom is a genuinely useful one to remember: strip comment lines and blank lines, and a four hundred line config file becomes the twelve lines someone actually changed.

Two practical matters to finish the fundamentals. First, shorthand classes. Backslash d for a digit, backslash w for a word character, backslash s for whitespace, and their capitalized forms for the negations. These are lovely and concise, but be aware they come from Perl, and plain grep does not understand them — you need grep dash capital P, or ripgrep, or a real programming language. The portable equivalents are the POSIX classes with their double square brackets, which look verbose but genuinely work everywhere including inside basic grep and sed. Second, and this one causes more confusion than any other single thing in this lesson: always wrap your pattern in single quotes. The shell processes your command line before grep ever sees it, and inside double quotes the shell will interpret backslashes, dollar signs and exclamation marks itself. So your carefully written pattern arrives at grep already mangled, and you get baffling results while staring at a pattern that looks perfectly correct. Single quotes tell the shell to pass the text through completely untouched. Make it an unconditional habit — single quotes around every regex, every time, even when it does not seem necessary. It costs nothing and removes an entire category of mystery.

Let us finish with method rather than syntax, because how you write a regex matters more than knowing every symbol. Never try to write the finished expression in one go. Build it in stages and test each stage. Suppose you want to find IP addresses in a log. Start with just a number. Refine it to one to three digits, which is an octet. Add a literal dot and a second octet, escaping the dot so it means an actual full stop. Notice the repetition, wrap the octet-and-dot in parentheses, and say it happens three times, then add the final octet. Five small steps, each one testable, and if a step breaks you know exactly which. The fastest way to test is echoing a sample string into grep, which gives you an instant feedback loop with no file needed. And notice grep dash o in there: it prints only the matching text rather than the whole line, which quietly turns grep from a filter into an extraction tool. Combined with the counting idiom, that one line pulls every IP out of a log and ranks them by frequency. Next lesson we add groups, alternation, and the greedy versus lazy distinction, which is where regex starts feeling genuinely powerful.
regex-practical: Parentheses solve the limitation from last lesson, where a quantifier only applied to the single character before it. Wrap something in parentheses and it becomes one unit, so a b in parentheses followed by plus means one or more repetitions of the pair a b, not an a followed by b's. That is grouping. Parentheses do a second job too — they capture what matched, so you can refer back to it, which the next slides use heavily. The vertical bar is alternation, meaning this or that. Inside a group it is enormously useful: ERROR or WARN or FATAL in parentheses matches a line starting with any of the three severity levels, which is a pattern you will write constantly when filtering logs. One precedence trap worth knowing, because it produces confusing results rather than errors. The alternation bar binds more loosely than everything else. So caret cat vertical bar dog does not mean a line starting with either cat or dog. It means either a line starting with cat, or the word dog appearing anywhere at all. Almost never what you intended. Wrap the alternatives in parentheses and the caret applies to both. And as before, plain grep wants backslashes before parentheses and bars, so reach for grep dash E and write them cleanly.

This is the single most common regex bug, and once you know it you will spot it instantly for the rest of your life. Quantifiers are greedy, meaning they grab as much text as they possibly can and only give some back if that is the only way to make the rest of the pattern match. Look at the example. You want to match an HTML tag, so you write less-than dot star greater-than, which reads as: a less-than, then anything, then a greater-than. Perfectly logical. But on a line containing several tags, the dot star swallows everything up to the very last greater-than on the line, so you match the entire line rather than one tag. There are two fixes. The lazy quantifier, a question mark after the star, tells it to match as little as possible instead — but that is a Perl-compatible feature, so it does not work in basic grep or sed. The portable fix is better anyway, and it is worth making your default: instead of saying anything, say anything that is not the closing character. Less-than, then a negated class of not-greater-than, then greater-than. It cannot overshoot because it physically cannot cross a greater-than sign. It also runs faster, because there is no backtracking. The same shape applies to quoted fields in logs, and that is the version you will use most.

Capturing is what turns regex from something that finds text into something that transforms text. When you wrap part of a pattern in parentheses, the regex engine remembers what that part actually matched, and you can refer back to it. Groups are numbered left to right by their opening parenthesis, so group one is the first open bracket you wrote. Inside the pattern itself, backslash one means match the same text that group one matched. That is how the doubled-word check on this slide works — a word, a space, then the same word again — which is a neat trick for catching the the in your own writing. But the real power shows up in sed, where you can use those captures in the replacement text. Look at the CSV example: capture everything up to the first comma as group one, capture the next field as group two, and then write them back in the opposite order. You have swapped two columns of a data file with one short expression. And the last line is the project-wide rename you will genuinely use: grep dash r l finds every file containing the old name, xargs feeds that list to sed, and sed rewrites each one in place. Word boundaries keep it from mangling longer names that merely contain your search term.

Here is the answer to a frustration you have probably already had: you copy a regex from the internet, it works in the online tester, and it does absolutely nothing in grep. The reason is that regex is not one language, it is three dialects. Basic regular expressions, which plain grep and sed use by default, are the oldest and most awkward — plus, parentheses and the alternation bar are all literal characters there, and you have to backslash them to get their special meaning, which is exactly backwards from what everyone expects. Extended regular expressions, which you get with dash E, fix that: those characters mean what they look like they should mean. Perl-compatible expressions, dash capital P, add the shorthand classes like backslash d and lazy quantifiers, plus lookahead and lookbehind. The practical advice is short. Use dash E by default in both grep and sed. It costs nothing, it removes all the backslash noise, and it is available everywhere. Reach for dash P only when you specifically need backslash d or lazy matching, and be aware that dash P is not compiled into grep on every system — notably not on macOS — so avoid it in scripts that other people will run on machines you have not seen.

Let us finish with the patterns worth keeping, because in practice nobody writes these fresh each time — they reuse them. Keep a snippets file somewhere you can find it, and add to it whenever you work one out. The ones here cover most of what logs throw at you: IP addresses, ISO timestamps, HTTP status codes in the four hundreds and five hundreds, a safely non-greedy quoted field, and key-equals-value configuration lines. Two closing pieces of judgement. First, email and URL matching are famously impossible to do fully correctly with a regex — the actual specifications are far more permissive than anyone expects, and every clever complete email regex you find online is either wrong or unreadable or both. Match loosely to find candidates, then validate properly with a real parser or by sending a confirmation. Do not try to be complete. Second, always test on real data, and specifically on the ugly lines: the truncated ones, the ones with unusual characters, the ones where a field is empty. A regex almost never fails on the input you imagined while writing it. It fails on the input you did not. Next lesson we take these patterns and start actually transforming text, with sed and awk.
scp-rsync-remote-files: Scp copies files over SSH and its syntax is deliberately familiar — it looks like cp, with a host and a colon in front of the remote path. It reads your SSH config, so the aliases you set up in the last lesson work here too, and copying to prod colon slash tmp just works. For a single file, scp is completely fine and it is installed everywhere. But be aware of its limits, because they matter as soon as the files get bigger. Scp has no concept of what is already there — it transfers everything, every time, so copying a directory twice means sending all the bytes twice. And it cannot resume: if your connection drops at ninety percent of a large transfer, you start again from zero. There is also a small annoyance worth memorizing now rather than discovering later: the port flag is a capital P, unlike ssh where it is lowercase. Lowercase p in scp means preserve timestamps, so getting it wrong does not give you a clear error, it just quietly fails to use the port you meant. For anything beyond a single file, use rsync instead — which is the rest of this lesson.

Rsync is the tool you should reach for almost every time, and its central idea is genuinely clever. Before transferring, it compares the two sides and works out what is actually different — not just which files, but which blocks within those files — and then sends only that. The practical consequence is dramatic. The first sync of a directory takes as long as you would expect. Every sync after that takes seconds, because almost nothing changed. If you deploy a site by copying a few hundred megabytes and only three files changed, rsync sends three files. Dash a is the flag to internalize, and it stands for archive mode. It is a bundle that means recurse into directories and preserve permissions, timestamps, symbolic links and ownership. That preservation matters more than people expect: copy a website without preserving permissions and your executable scripts arrive non-executable, which produces a very confusing broken deployment. Dash z compresses data in transit, which is a clear win over any slow link and roughly neutral on a fast local network. And dash capital P combines progress display with partial transfer support, so a big copy can resume where it stopped rather than starting over. Use it on anything large.

This tiny detail causes more rsync confusion than everything else combined, so let us fix it permanently. A trailing slash on the source path means copy the contents of this directory. No trailing slash means copy this directory itself. So source-slash to dest puts the files directly in dest, while source without a slash to dest creates a folder named source inside dest and puts the files in there. Get it wrong on a deployment and you end up with slash s r v slash app slash app, with your application one level deeper than the web server is looking, and a confusing few minutes follow. Everyone does this at least once. The trailing slash on the destination, incidentally, makes no difference at all — only the source matters. And here is the habit that protects you from this and from much worse: dash n, the dry run flag. Combined with dash v it prints exactly what rsync would transfer and delete, and changes nothing. Run it, read the list, and only then run the real command. This is the same discipline as running ls before rm, and it matters even more here, because the next slide is about a flag that deletes files.

Dash dash delete makes the destination exactly mirror the source, which means it removes any file at the destination that is not present in the source. That is genuinely what you want for a deployment, because otherwise files you deleted from your project linger on the server forever, and old versions of scripts hanging around is a real source of confusion and occasionally of security problems. But treat this flag with the same respect as rm dash r f, because in the wrong circumstances it is exactly that. Point it at the wrong destination directory and it will faithfully delete everything there that is not in your source. Combine it with the trailing slash mistake from the last slide and the damage can be considerable. So the rule is absolute: never run dash dash delete without running it with dash n first and reading the output. There is no exception to this rule that is worth the risk. On excludes: add them before you introduce dash dash delete, not after — because if you exclude a directory from the transfer while dash dash delete is active, rsync will happily remove it at the destination for not being in the source. Excluding dot git and node modules typically cuts a deployment transfer by ninety percent, so it is worth doing regardless of speed.

Let us finish with patterns you can use directly. The deploy line is the everyday one: push your built site, delete anything stale on the server, and skip the git directory. Pulling logs down is the reverse and it is often the most comfortable way to analyse a problem — get the logs onto your own machine where you have your tools, rather than working in a cramped SSH session. But the third example is the one I want you to appreciate, because it connects back to a concept from Part One. With dash dash link dest, rsync creates a new dated backup directory, but for every file that has not changed since the previous backup, it creates a hard link to the existing copy rather than a new copy of the data. Remember hard links: two names pointing at the same inode, with the data stored only once. So you end up with thirty dated directories, each one appearing to be a complete full backup you can browse and restore from directly, while the actual disk cost is one full copy plus only the changes. That is how professional snapshot backup systems work underneath, and you now have it in one command. That is also a nice demonstration of why the fundamentals in this course were worth learning — this trick is unremarkable once you know what an inode is, and pure magic if you do not.
sed-awk: Sed is a stream editor. It reads input line by line, applies your instructions, and writes the result out, which means it can edit a file of ten million lines without ever loading it into memory. Ninety percent of sed usage is one command: s, for substitute, written as s slash old slash new slash. The single most important detail is the g flag on the end. Without it, sed replaces only the first match on each line, and this surprises people constantly — you run a substitution, most of the text changes, and you cannot work out why some instances survived. They survived because they were the second occurrence on their line. Add g and it replaces all of them. A genuinely useful trick: the delimiter does not have to be a forward slash. It can be any character, so when you are rewriting file paths, use a pipe or a comma instead and you avoid having to escape every slash in the path. That turns an unreadable thicket of backslashes into something you can actually check. Sed can also delete lines matching a pattern, print only a range, and insert text. And dash n turns off the automatic printing of every line, which is what makes the print command selective rather than doubling everything.

Dash i makes sed edit the file in place rather than printing to your screen, and it is simultaneously the most useful and most dangerous flag in this lesson. There is no undo. If your expression is subtly wrong, you have just silently corrupted a file, and if you ran it across a whole project with xargs, you have corrupted hundreds. So adopt this discipline permanently: run the command without dash i first. Sed will print the transformed output and change nothing, and you can read it, or better, pipe it into diff against the original to see exactly which lines would change. Only when that diff looks right do you add dash i. The second protection costs nothing at all: dash i dot bak keeps a copy of the original alongside the edited file. It has rescued a great many afternoons and there is no reason not to use it. One portability wrinkle that will bite you if you move between machines. GNU sed on Linux takes dash i with nothing after it. BSD sed on macOS requires an argument for the backup suffix, so you have to write dash i followed by an empty pair of quotes. A script written on one silently fails or misbehaves on the other, and this is one of the most common cross-platform annoyances in shell scripting.

Awk is the tool for text that has columns, and its central convenience is that it splits every line into fields for you automatically. Dollar one is the first field, dollar two the second, dollar N F is the last one whatever the count, and dollar zero is the whole line. You do not have to write any parsing. Dash capital F sets the separator when it is not whitespace, which is how you handle colon-separated system files or comma-separated data. The structure of the language is just pattern brace action brace, and both parts are optional, which explains programs that look strange at first. If you give only an action, it runs on every line. If you give only a pattern, the default action is to print the line — which is why awk with dollar three greater than one hundred, with no braces at all, is a complete working program that prints every row where the third column exceeds a hundred. Two built-in variables you will use constantly: N R is the current line number, and N F is how many fields this line has. N R equals one is how you keep a header row, and N F is how you spot malformed lines with too few columns. Learn those two and a great deal of awk becomes readable.

This is where awk stops being a field extractor and becomes genuinely a small programming language. It has variables that need no declaration — mention one and it exists, starting at zero or empty string. It has BEGIN and END blocks, which run before the first line and after the last, and END is where you print totals once everything has been counted. So summing a column is one short line: add field three to a running total on every line, then print the total at the end. The last example is the one worth really understanding, because it is a complete group-by in a single line. Awk has associative arrays, meaning arrays indexed by strings rather than numbers. So count square bracket dollar one, plus plus, uses the first field — an IP address, say — as the key, and increments a counter for it. After every line has been read, the END block loops over the array and prints each key with its count. That is exactly what a GROUP BY does in SQL, over a log file, with no database, in about forty characters. Pipe it into sort and you have your top talkers. Once this clicks, you will find yourself reaching for awk instead of writing a Python script surprisingly often.

Let us finish by drawing the boundaries, because the tools overlap and knowing which to reach for is most of the fluency. Grep finds the lines you care about. Sed rewrites text within lines. Awk works with columns and can count and compute. Cut grabs a single fixed field and is simpler and faster than awk when that is genuinely all you need — though awk handles messy, ragged whitespace much better, which real log files are full of. Sort and uniq order and count. The example at the bottom is the classic team playing together: grep narrows to the requests you care about, awk pulls out the three columns that matter, and the counting idiom ranks them. Four tools, one line, and an answer you would otherwise have written a script for. Now, one piece of honest judgement to close on. There is a line past which these tools stop being the right answer. If you find yourself writing a thirty-line awk program with functions and nested logic, you have crossed it — write Python instead, where you get real data structures, error handling, and something a colleague can read next year. Awk is brilliant for one-liners and poor for programs. Knowing where that line sits is itself a senior skill.
shell-environment: Let us start with the thing that wastes hours: which configuration file actually gets read, because the answer depends on how the shell was started and it is genuinely confusing. A login shell — what you get when you SSH in or log in at a console — reads bash underscore profile. An interactive non-login shell — a new terminal tab on your desktop — reads bashrc. Those are different files, and that single fact explains the classic complaint that an alias works in one terminal but not over SSH. The standard fix, which nearly every real dotfile setup uses, is to have bash profile source bashrc, so both paths end up loading the same configuration and you only maintain one file. Zsh sidesteps most of this: zshrc runs for effectively everything. And here is the part that matters most for the rest of Part Four. Scripts and cron jobs read neither file. A non-interactive shell loads no configuration at all. So your aliases do not exist inside a script, your customized PATH may not exist, and a command that works perfectly when you type it can fail under cron. That is not a bug, it is the design — and knowing it turns a mystifying failure into an obvious one.

When you type a command, the shell does something very simple: it walks through the directories listed in your PATH variable, left to right, and runs the first matching executable it finds. That is the whole mechanism. PATH is nothing more than a colon-separated list of directories, and understanding that order is left to right and first match wins explains almost every version confusion you will ever have. When you are certain you installed a newer Python but the old one keeps starting, the old one lives in a directory that appears earlier in your PATH. Which tells you the winner; type is better still, because it also reveals if the name is actually an alias or a shell function rather than a program on disk. To add a directory, export a new PATH that includes it — and the position matters. Put your directory first if you want your version to override the system one; put it last to add tools without shadowing anything. One firm security rule to close on: never put a bare dot, meaning the current directory, in your PATH. If you do, then changing into a directory someone else can write to and typing ls could run their program called ls instead of the real one. It is a classic privilege escalation, and the convenience is not worth it.

There are two kinds of variable and the distinction matters constantly. A plain assignment creates a shell variable, which exists only in the shell you typed it in. Adding export promotes it to an environment variable, which means every program the shell starts from then on inherits it. So if you set a variable without export and then run a script that expects it, the script sees nothing — and this is one of the most common confusions in early scripting. There is also a neat shorthand: putting the assignment directly in front of a command sets it for that one command only, which is perfect for a temporary debug flag. Now the deeper point, and it explains a behaviour that puzzles people. Children inherit a copy of the environment, not a shared reference. A child process can change its own copy all it likes and the parent never sees it. That is precisely why a script cannot change your current directory: it runs in a child shell, it changes that child's directory, and then the child exits and takes the change with it. When you genuinely want a script to modify your current shell — to set variables or move you somewhere — you must source it rather than run it, which executes it inside your existing shell instead of a new one.

Aliases are simple text substitution: the shell sees the alias name and swaps in the text before running anything. They are perfect for shortening commands you type dozens of times a day — l l for a detailed listing, g s for git status. But because they are pure substitution, they cannot take arguments in any useful way. The moment you need a parameter, write a function instead. The mkcd example on this slide is one worth stealing: it makes a directory and immediately changes into it, which is something you do constantly and the shell inexplicably has no built-in for. A note on aliasing rm to rm dash i. It genuinely does protect you, and plenty of people do it. But be aware of the trade: you build a reflex that expects a confirmation prompt, and that reflex does not transfer to servers where the alias is not configured. You may be safer at home and less careful everywhere else. Decide deliberately. Two practical bits: alias with no arguments lists everything currently defined, which is useful on an unfamiliar account, and prefixing any command with a backslash bypasses an alias for that one invocation, which is how you get the real rm when you actually want it.

Let us finish with a bashrc actually worth having, focusing on the settings that pay off rather than a long list. The history settings first, because they are the most undervalued lines here. By default bash keeps a small history and, worse, multiple terminal tabs overwrite each other's history file when they close, so you lose commands. Setting a large history size and enabling histappend fixes both. Combine that with Control R searching and your own past becomes documentation — that complicated ffmpeg invocation you worked out eight months ago is still there, and you never have to derive it twice. That is a genuinely large productivity gain for three lines of configuration. Then the small quality-of-life ones: cdspell fixes typos in directory names automatically, checkwinsize keeps things laid out correctly after you resize the window, and colouring grep makes matches visible at a glance. Set EDITOR so that every tool that needs to open an editor opens the one you want. And the closing advice, which is the highest-leverage thing in this lesson: keep your dotfiles in a git repository. Then setting up a brand new machine, or a fresh server, is one clone away from feeling exactly like home — and you never lose that configuration again.
ssh-fundamentals: Key-based authentication is worth understanding rather than just following the steps, because the mechanism is genuinely clever and knowing it makes the security properties obvious. You generate a pair of mathematically related keys. The private one stays on your machine forever. The public one you copy to any server you want to reach. When you connect, the server does not ask for your key. It sends your client a random challenge, your client signs that challenge using the private key, and the server verifies the signature against the public key it already has. Your private key is never transmitted, not even in encrypted form. Sit with what that gives you: even if a server you connect to is completely compromised, the attacker learns nothing they can use to impersonate you elsewhere, because they only ever saw a signature over a random value. Compare that with a password, which you hand over in full to every server you log into. That is why key authentication is not merely more convenient than passwords — it is a fundamentally stronger design. Use ed25519 rather than RSA: the keys are much shorter, verification is faster, and there is no key-size decision you can get wrong. And remember from the permissions lesson that SSH refuses a private key others can read, so chmod six zero zero.

If you take one practical action from this lesson, make it writing this file, because it is the single biggest quality-of-life improvement available to anyone who uses SSH regularly. Instead of remembering an IP address, a non-standard port, a username and a key path, you define a short alias once and then type ssh prod. And the benefits go well beyond typing less. Scp, rsync, and git all read the same config file, so defining a host once means every tool that talks over SSH now knows how to reach it. ProxyJump is the entry worth highlighting. In real infrastructure, database servers usually live on a private network with no public address, and you reach them by hopping through a bastion host. Without config, that is a tedious two-step every time. With ProxyJump, you type ssh db and SSH silently connects to the bastion, tunnels through it, and lands you on the database server, as though it were directly reachable. The Host star block at the bottom applies to everything: ServerAliveInterval sends a small keepalive every sixty seconds, which stops idle connections being dropped by firewalls and routers — that annoying frozen terminal after you step away for coffee.

Always put a passphrase on your private key. The reason is simple: without one, anyone who copies that file — a stolen laptop, a bad backup, a misconfigured sync folder — has your access to every server. With a passphrase, the file alone is useless to them. The obvious objection is that typing a passphrase on every connection would be unbearable, and that is exactly what the agent solves. Ssh-add unlocks the key once and hands it to the agent, which holds it in memory. From then on, when a server sends a challenge, your client asks the agent to sign it. The agent signs and returns the signature; it never gives the key itself to anything. So you get passphrase protection with the convenience of no passphrase. On macOS you can store it in the Keychain so it persists across reboots. Now agent forwarding, dash capital A, deserves a caution. It lets a server you are connected to use your local agent to authenticate onward — genuinely useful for pulling from a private git repository on a remote box. But while that connection is open, anyone with root on that server can use your agent to authenticate as you, anywhere your keys work. Only forward to hosts you genuinely trust, and prefer ProxyJump, which achieves most of the same convenience without the exposure.

Two server-side matters. First, hardening. Turning off password authentication entirely is the single highest-value change you can make to an internet-facing server, because it removes brute-forcing as a category of threat — attackers can hammer port twenty-two forever and there is simply no password to guess. Disable direct root login too, so people log in as themselves and then escalate with sudo, which gives you the audit trail we discussed earlier. Now the safety procedure, and please take this one seriously: always run sshd dash t to validate the config before reloading, and keep your current SSH session open while you test a brand new connection in a separate terminal. If you have made a mistake, that existing session is your only way back in. People have locked themselves out of production servers by reloading a broken sshd config and closing their terminal, and the recovery involves a console session through the cloud provider, if you are lucky. Second, that alarming warning about the remote host identification having changed. It means the server's host key no longer matches what your client recorded, and it exists to detect a machine-in-the-middle attack. Usually it is innocent — the server was rebuilt. But verify that is actually the case before you clear the entry with ssh-keygen dash capital R.

Tunnels are the feature that makes people say SSH is remarkable, and there is one you will genuinely use. A local forward, dash capital L, takes a port on a remote network and makes it appear on your own machine. The classic case: your production database listens only on the internal network and has no public address, quite rightly. With one command you map your local port fifty-four thirty-three to the database's port through the SSH connection, and then you point your graphical database client at localhost fifty-four thirty-three and it just works. The traffic travels encrypted inside the SSH connection, and you never had to expose the database to the internet. The syntax reads awkwardly, so here is the trick for remembering it: the first number is the port on your machine, and the host and port after it are written from the server's point of view. So localhost in that middle position means localhost as the server sees it — the server itself. Change it to a private IP and you reach a third machine that only the server can talk to, which is how you tunnel through a bastion into a locked-down network. Dash capital R does the reverse, exposing something of yours on the server, which is occasionally handy for demos and webhooks. And dash f capital N puts the tunnel in the background without opening a shell.
systemd-services: Systemd is the first process the kernel starts, PID one, and it is the ancestor of everything else on the machine. Its job is to start services in the right order, keep them running, restart them when they crash, and collect their logs. You talk to it with systemctl, and the commands are mostly self-explanatory: start, stop, restart, and status. But there is one distinction on this slide that catches nearly everybody at least once, so let us make it stick. Start runs a service right now, in this moment, and that is all it does. Enable makes a service start automatically at every future boot, and it does not start it now. They are completely independent. So you can start a service, confirm it works, be satisfied, and then discover weeks later after a reboot that it never came back — because you started it but never enabled it. The reverse also happens: you enable something and wonder why nothing is running. The command that does both is enable dash dash now, and it is worth making that your default. Also notice reload versus restart: reload asks the service to re-read its configuration while continuing to serve, whereas restart stops and starts it, dropping every connection. For a busy web server that difference is very visible to your users.

Status is the command you will run most, so let us read its output properly, because two different facts live in there and people routinely conflate them. The Loaded line tells you about boot behaviour — where the unit file is and whether the service is enabled, meaning whether it will start after a reboot. The Active line tells you about right now: is it running, has it stopped, did it fail. Those are independent. A service can be enabled but not currently active because it crashed, or active but not enabled because someone started it by hand and it will silently not return after the next reboot. Read both lines every time. One state that confuses people is active in brackets exited. That is not an error. It means the unit ran a one-shot task, like configuring a network interface or applying firewall rules, and finished successfully. It was never meant to keep running. The other genuinely useful thing about status is that it prints the last several log lines from the service at the bottom. When something has failed, look there first — a very high proportion of the time the answer is sitting right in front of you, and people go hunting through log files without noticing it was already printed.

Under systemd, service logs do not necessarily go into files in var log any more. Systemd captures whatever a service writes to standard output and standard error and stores it in a structured binary journal, which you query with journalctl. This is genuinely convenient once you accept it: your application does not need to implement logging to a file, or handle rotation, or worry about permissions. It just prints, and systemd catches it. The flag you will use constantly is dash u followed by the unit name, which filters to just that service. Add dash f and you get live following, exactly like tail dash f but for a service. Dash n limits how many lines, dash dash since takes plain English time expressions like ten minutes ago, and dash p err filters to only errors and worse, which is how you cut through a very noisy service. The one I especially want you to remember is dash b minus one. Dash b shows logs from the current boot, and minus one shows the previous boot. So when a server has rebooted unexpectedly and you want to know what happened in the moments before it went down, that is the command. And do check journalctl dash dash disk usage occasionally, because the journal grows and is a common reason var fills up.

Here is where this becomes genuinely useful to you: turning your own application into a real service. Drop a unit file in etc systemd system and you get, for about twelve lines of configuration, automatic start at boot, automatic restart on crash, log collection, and a standard way for anyone to control it. Walk through the sections. Unit holds the description and ordering — After network target simply means do not start this until networking is up. Service is the substance. User runs it as an unprivileged account, and this should never be root. ExecStart is the command, and it must be an absolute path, because systemd does not run a shell and there is no PATH to search — this is the single most common mistake in a first unit file. Restart on failure is the line that earns its keep: if your process crashes, systemd brings it back, five seconds later in this example. And the Install section is what enable hooks into, so without it enable has nothing to do. One gotcha to internalize: after you edit a unit file, systemd does not notice by itself. You must run systemctl daemon dash reload and then restart the service. If your changes seem to have no effect, that is almost always why.

Let us close with the debugging sequence, because your first unit file will not work and that is completely normal. Start with status, read the failure line, and look at the log excerpt it prints. Then journalctl dash u with dash n fifty for the real error in more detail. If nothing there is obvious, systemd analyze verify checks the unit file for typos and invalid directives, which catches the embarrassing ones quickly. But the fourth step is the one that finds most problems, and I would reach for it early: run the ExecStart command yourself, manually, as the service user, using sudo dash u. Almost every failing unit fails for a reason that shows up immediately when you do this — the virtual environment path is wrong, the user cannot read a config file, a directory does not exist, an environment variable is missing. You see the real error in your terminal instead of inferring it from the outside. Two specific things worth recognizing: a status of two-oh-three slash EXEC means systemd could not execute the binary at all, so the path is wrong or the file is not executable. And systemctl cat shows you the unit as systemd actually sees it, including any drop-in overrides, which is how you discover that a file you did not know about has been quietly changing your configuration.
terminal-first-commands: Three words get used interchangeably and they are genuinely three different things, so let us separate them once, properly. The terminal is the window. It is a dumb display, really — it draws text on your screen and captures your keystrokes. That is its whole job. The shell is the program running inside that window. It reads what you type, works out what you meant, runs it, and shows you the result. Bash and zsh are shells. And the prompt is the little bit of text the shell prints to tell you it is finished with the last thing and ready for the next. Why bother distinguishing them? Because when you SSH into a server in Part Five, the terminal stays on your laptop while the shell is running two thousand kilometres away. If those two are one blurry concept in your head, that moment is confusing. If you have kept them separate, it is obvious: your window, their shell. Think of the terminal as the telephone handset and the shell as the person on the other end actually doing what you ask.

Take a proper look at the prompt, because it is not decoration — it is a status display, and once you are managing more than one machine it is the thing that saves you. Read it left to right. First your username: who the system thinks you are, which decides what you are allowed to touch. Then, after the at sign, the hostname: which machine you are on. Then the current directory, where a tilde is shorthand for your home folder. And finally the symbol: a dollar sign means you are a normal user, while a hash means you are root and every mistake you make is now permanent and system-wide. Here is why I am spending a whole slide on this. Once you start SSH-ing, you will have several terminal tabs open, and some of them are your laptop and some of them are production. The hostname in that prompt is the only thing standing between a routine cleanup command and deleting the wrong machine's files. Experienced people read the prompt before every dangerous command, the way a driver checks the mirror. Build that habit now, while nothing is at stake.

Almost every command you will ever type has the same three-part shape, and once you see it you stop memorizing commands and start reading them. First the command itself — the program to run. Then options, also called flags, which change how it behaves. Then arguments: what to act on. Flags come in two styles. A single dash takes a single letter, and you can bundle several together, so dash l dash a becomes dash l a. A double dash takes a whole word — dash dash all — which is longer to type but tells anyone reading your script exactly what you meant. Use short flags when you are typing live and long flags when you are writing something another person will read. Now, one detail that will bite you within your first week: the shell splits what you type on spaces. That is how it knows where the command ends and the arguments begin. So a file genuinely named My Notes dot txt looks like two separate arguments, and the command fails in a confusing way. The fix is quoting, and we will meet it properly in the scripting lessons — but file this away now, because that is the error you will hit first.

Here is the honest short list. Not every command in Linux — the ones you will genuinely type, dozens of times a day, for the rest of your career. Pwd tells you where you are. Ls with dash l a shows you what is here including the hidden dotfiles, and hidden files matter on Linux because that is where all the configuration lives. Cd moves you around, and cd with just a dash is a lovely one: it snaps you back to the directory you were in before, like the back button in a browser. Man opens the manual — press q to quit and forward slash to search inside it — and if the manual page feels overwhelming, ls dash dash help gives you the short version. History shows what you ran before. Now let me point at the two things that separate someone who is fluent in a terminal from someone who is fighting it. First, tab completion: start typing a path, press Tab, and the shell finishes it. This is not about saving keystrokes, it is about never mistyping a path. Second, Control R: press it and start typing any fragment of a command you ran before, and the shell finds it. Learn those two today and you will thank yourself for years.

Let us finish with the idea that ties the whole system together, because it will keep paying off for the rest of the course. In Linux, everything is a file. Not just documents — your keyboard is a file, your screen is a file, your hard disk is a file, a network connection is a file, and a running process is a directory full of files. This sounds like a strange philosophical claim until you see what it buys you. Because everything looks like a file, the same small set of tools works on all of it. The commands you learn for reading a text file also read your CPU information, also read a running process's memory usage, also send data to another machine. Try this one when you have a terminal open: cat slash proc slash cpuinfo. You will get a full description of your processor. But there is no such file on your disk. When you read it, the kernel manufactures that text on the spot and hands it to you, because it is pretending to be a file so that ordinary tools can talk to it. That is the deepest design idea in Unix, and you now have it. Next lesson, we walk the filesystem itself and learn why the directories are named what they are.
users-groups-sudo: Here is something that explains a surprising amount once you know it: the kernel has no idea what your username is. It works entirely in numbers. Every user is a UID, every group is a GID, and the names exist purely so humans can read them. When you run ls dash l and see your name next to a file, a lookup just happened, translating the number stored on disk into text for your benefit. The file doing that translation is etc passwd, and despite the name it contains no passwords — it holds one line per user with the UID, the primary group, the home directory, and the login shell. The x in the second field is a leftover from when the password hash genuinely did sit there; today it points you at etc shadow, which is readable only by root. That split exists because etc passwd needs to be world-readable for name lookups to work, and you obviously cannot have password hashes in a world-readable file. And the detail worth carrying with you: UID zero is root. It is the number that grants unlimited power, not the name. An account called anything at all with UID zero is root, which is a classic thing to check for when auditing a machine you have inherited.

Groups are how several people get access to the same thing without anyone sharing a password or becoming root. You have one primary group, which is what new files you create belong to, and any number of supplementary groups that grant extra access. Adding someone to a group is usermod dash a G, and I want to stop on that dash a because it is one of the genuinely dangerous typos in Linux administration. The dash G flag sets a user's supplementary groups to exactly the list you give. The dash a makes it append instead. So if you type usermod dash G docker talank, meaning to add yourself to docker, you have just replaced every group you were in with only docker — including sudo. You have removed your own administrative access, and if you are working over SSH with no other way in, you have locked yourself out of the machine. Always dash a G. Always. And a smaller gotcha that wastes a lot of people's time: group membership is read when you log in, so after adding yourself to a group, your current shell still has the old list. Log out and back in, or the change appears not to have worked at all.

Sudo lets you borrow root's authority for a single command instead of living as root, and the reasons to prefer it are stronger than they first appear. First, accident containment: as root, every typo is potentially catastrophic, and rm with a stray space stops being an inconvenience and becomes a rebuild. Running as yourself means the system refuses most of your mistakes for free. Second, and this matters on any machine more than one person touches: sudo logs every command it runs, with who ran it and when, to the authentication log. A root shell logs nothing — you get one line saying a root session started, and then silence. When something breaks at three in the morning, that log is how you find out what actually happened. Third, sudo asks for your own password, not root's, which means the root account can have no password at all and there is no shared secret to leak or rotate when someone leaves. A few practical notes. Sudo dash l shows what you are permitted to do. Sudo bang bang re-runs the command you just typed with sudo, which is the fix for the daily ritual of forgetting it. And always edit the sudoers file with visudo, never directly, because visudo checks your syntax before saving — a malformed sudoers file can lock every administrator out of the machine at once.

Look at any real server with ps and you will notice something deliberate. Nginx has a master process running as root and worker processes running as a user called www-data, and it is the workers that actually handle requests from the internet. This pattern is called dropping privileges and it is one of the most important security ideas in server administration. The master needs root for exactly one thing: binding to port eighty, because ports below one thousand and twenty-four are restricted. The moment that is done, it hands the real work to unprivileged workers and keeps only the supervisory role for itself. So when someone finds a vulnerability in your web application, what they get is the www-data account, which can read the site files and very little else — not root, not your machine. Look at that account in etc passwd and notice its login shell is set to nologin. That is not a real shell; it is a small program whose only behaviour is to refuse and exit. So even if an attacker somehow obtains that account's credentials, they cannot open a session with it. Service accounts exist to be a dead end. When you deploy your own applications, run them the same way — never as root, always as a dedicated nologin user.

Let us finish with the commands you will genuinely reach for. Id tells you who you actually are including every group, and it is the right first command when something is unexpectedly denied. Sudo dash l tells you what you are permitted to do. Getent looks a user up properly, and it is worth preferring over grepping etc passwd, because on a machine joined to a company directory the users may not be in that file at all — getent asks the whole name resolution system, so it finds them either way. Adduser creates accounts interactively and handles the home directory and defaults for you. And the last one is real-world advice more than a command. When someone leaves the team, the instinct is to delete their account. Do not. Their UID still owns files all over the machine, and deleting the user leaves those files owned by a bare number with no name, which is confusing forever afterwards, and worse, a future user created with that same recycled UID silently inherits ownership of all of them. Lock the account instead, with passwd dash l. They cannot log in, nothing breaks, and the ownership record stays readable.
why-linux-matters: Let's clear up something that confuses people for years, because casual speech never distinguishes it. Linux, strictly speaking, is one program: the kernel, started by Linus Torvalds in 1991. It is the layer that talks to the actual hardware — it decides which process gets the CPU next, it manages memory, it hands out access to disks and network cards. On its own a kernel is not something you use. There is no prompt, no ls command, nothing to log into. What you actually install and use is a distribution: the kernel, plus the core command-line tools, plus a package manager, plus a set of defaults and conventions. Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Red Hat, Arch, Alpine — all different distributions wrapped around the same kernel. And this is genuinely good news for you, because it means the question people agonize over, which distro should I learn, is close to a non-question. You are about to learn the ninety percent that is identical everywhere. Where they diverge — mostly which package manager they use — this course calls it out explicitly.

Linux inherited its design DNA from Unix, built at Bell Labs in the nineteen-seventies, and one idea from that era explains almost every tool in this course. Write small programs that each do one thing well, that read text and write text, and let people combine them. Look at how narrow these tools are. Grep only searches text. Sort only sorts lines. Word count only counts. None of them knows the others exist. But because every one of them speaks the same language — plain text in, plain text out — you can chain them together with a pipe into combinations that no single tool's author ever imagined. This is a genuinely different instinct from a big graphical application that tries to do everything inside itself. Think of it like a Nepali kitchen: you do not own one machine that makes dal bhat. You own a pressure cooker, a tawa, a khukuri, a chalni — each simple, each good at one job, and the cook combines them into any meal. That is the shell. And it is why a huge share of how do I do this questions collapse into which two or three small tools do I chain together.

Your laptop might run macOS or Windows, but the machine your code deploys to almost certainly does not. The reasons are concrete, not just tradition. Linux is free and open source, which matters enormously when you are running ten thousand servers and would otherwise pay a licence for each one. It is extremely stable running headless — no graphical interface, just quietly serving, for months at a time. Every cloud provider defaults their images to it. And here is the reason that matters most for where this course is heading: Docker containers are Linux processes, using Linux-specific kernel features called namespaces and cgroups, which get a full lesson in Part Seven. There is no such thing as a Windows container running the same way. When you run Docker on a Mac, it is quietly starting a Linux virtual machine underneath and running your container in there. So put it together. Your pipeline runs on Linux. The containers it builds are Linux. The Kubernetes nodes that schedule them are Linux boxes. When you SSH in at eleven at night to find out why a deploy failed, you are on a Linux box using exactly the tools this course teaches.

Good news for starting today: macOS is Unix — BSD-flavoured rather than Linux, but a close cousin — so the Terminal app already on your machine runs a real shell, and most of what you learn through Part Four behaves identically. You need to install nothing to begin. There are a few small differences and I would rather you hear them from me now than be ambushed later. macOS ships the BSD versions of some tools, notably ls and sed, and their flags differ slightly from the GNU versions that Linux servers use. Wherever that bites, the lesson calls it out as a pitfall rather than leaving you to discover it at a bad moment. Then Part Five is where this stops being a simulation. You will set up a real SSH connection to an actual Linux machine — a cheap cloud VM, a Raspberry Pi, or a spare box; the lesson walks through the options — and from that point everything runs for real, on a real remote Linux machine. Which is exactly the day-to-day reality this whole course is preparing you for.

Let me end with why this course exists at all, sitting where it does, right before the Docker and Kubernetes one. You could skip straight to learning Docker. Plenty of people do. They learn the commands, the pipeline works, and then one day something breaks in a way the tutorial did not cover — a permission denied inside the container, a process that will not die, a mount that is empty — and there is no foundation underneath to reason from. Here is the sentence this whole course is quietly building toward: a container is not magic, it is a Linux process. It is an ordinary process that the kernel has lied to, using namespaces, so that it sees its own filesystem, its own network, its own process IDs — and that cgroups have fenced in, so it cannot eat all the memory. That is it. That is the trick. Once you know what a process is, what a filesystem is, what a permission is, and what a namespace is, Docker stops being a black box you memorize and becomes a thin, sensible convenience over things you already understand. So: next lesson, we open the terminal and type our first commands. Let's begin.
